# GluN2B-specific NMDAR positive allosteric modulation reverses cognitive and behavioral abnormalities in Mecp2 and Disc1 transgenic mice

**Authors:** Yang Ge; Tian Tian; Bolong Li; Peter Axerio-Cillies; Wenlin Chen; Xin Qin; Mudi Zhao; Qi-Cheng Sun; Jiaqi Li; Stan B. Floresco; Lidong Liu; Xin Yang; Yu Tian Wang

**Affiliations:** 1Djavad Mowafaghian Centre for Brain Health and Department of Medicine, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC V6T 2B5, Canada. | 2Faculty of Life and Health Sciences, Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology, Shenzhen, PR China. | 3Shenzhen Key Laboratory of Translational Research for Brain Diseases, Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shenzhen, PR China. | 4Fudan-SANS Neuroscience Center, Fudan University, Shanghai, PR China. | 5School of Finance, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, PR China.

## Abstract

The GluN2B subunit of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) plays a central role in synaptic development and plasticity, and its hypofunction is linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), severe neurodevelopmental delay, and other neuropsychiatric diseases. Therefore, enhancing the function of this NMDAR subunit may provide an effective therapeutic strategy for correcting synaptic and behavioral deficits associated with GluN2B hypofunction. Here, we developed a class of GluN2B-selective positive allosteric modulators and characterized the pharmacological properties and binding site of the lead compound, 175. Systemic application of 175 facilitates hippocampal long-term depression in rats. 175 restores performances in open-field exploration and three-chamber test in Mecp2 overexpression mice that exhibit GluN2B hypofunction and autism-like features. Treatment with 175 also reverses behavioral abnormalities in open-field, Y-maze spontaneous alternation, three-chamber test, and prepulse inhibition in Disc1 mutant mice. Our findings introduce a pharmacological tool for selectively potentiating GluN2B-NMDAR function and highlight its therapeutic potential for cognitive and behavioral symptoms associated with GluN2B hypofunction.

## Abstract

Development of GluN2B-selective NMDA receptor enhancers restores behavior in mouse models of neuropsychiatric disorders.

## INTRODUCTION

Hypofunction of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) has been recognized as a key pathological mechanism in neuropsychiatric diseases (1, 2). Rare loss-of-function variants in several genes encoding NMDAR subunits, including GRIN2B and GRIN2A, are robustly associated with the risks of developing autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (3, 4) and schizophrenia (5, 6) in humans, respectively. Moreover, both acute and subchronic treatments with NMDAR-antagonist ketamine or phencyclidine induce psychotic-like symptoms in humans and rodent models (1, 7–11). Therefore, reversing the hypofunction of NMDA-type glutamate receptors may be a promising strategy for treating the symptoms of these diseases.

NMDARs are tetraheteromeric protein complexes formed by two obligatory GluN1 subunits and two GluN2/3 subunits (12). The predominant GluN2/3 subunits expressed in most forebrain regions are GluN2A and GluN2B, rendering diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A-, GluN1/GluN2B-, and triheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B-NMDARs—the most dominant forms of NMDAR complexes in these regions (12, 13). However, the relative expression levels of diheteromeric and triheteromeric NMDARs remain a topic of debate (14).

The GluN2B subunit plays a critical role in synaptic development and plasticity, and its hypofunction is linked to neurodevelopmental disorders and deficits in synaptic function and plasticity (15, 16). Notably, a landmark human genetic study identified GRIN2B, the human gene encoding the GluN2B subunit, as one of the top significant genes whose loss of function confers substantial risks of developing ASD (3). Furthermore, multiple transgenic mouse models of ASD including shank3, shank2, and P-Rex1 mutant mice all had GluN2B hypofunction (17–19), implicating the GluN2B loss of function as a converging pathogenic mechanism in ASD. One physiological mechanism linking the GluN2B subunit to neurodevelopmental diseases, including but not limited to ASD, is its role in the induction of synaptic plasticity, especially long-term depression (LTD) (14). Transgenic mice carrying conditional homozygous knockout or heterozygous loss-of-function mutation of the GluN2B subunit develop impaired hippocampal LTD induced by electrical stimulations (4, 16, 20, 21). Enhancement of NMDAR functions by d-serine or d-cycloserine facilitates GluN2B-dependent LTD in wild-type (WT) mice (22) and restores impaired LTD in a transgenic mouse model harboring heterozygous GluN2B-Cys456→Tyr (C456Y) mutation derived from patients with ASD (4).

LTD has been one of the best-characterized synaptic mechanisms underlying behaviors that require the flexible use of information, including spatial working memory (16, 21), memory forgetting (23, 24), spatial reversal learning (22, 25, 26), fear extinction (27, 28), and latent inhibition (29). Moreover, loss of the GluN2B subunit in animal models has been associated with abnormal anxiety levels and impaired social function (15, 21). We therefore reasoned that GluN2B-containing NMDARs could serve as viable targets for treating these cognitive and behavioral symptoms in a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental diseases.

Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) targeting NMDARs have been rapidly developed as therapeutics for various neuropsychiatric indications (30–34). Compared with drugs that act on agonist or coagonist binding sites, PAMs, which target the allosteric binding sites, offer several advantages, including diverse modes of action, fewer side effects, and greater potential for subtype specificity (35–37). Nevertheless, the only GluN2B-containing NMDAR–specific PAMs reported are polyamines, which are limited by their low potency and poor specificity against non-NMDAR targets (38, 39).

To investigate whether enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR function would alleviate symptoms related to impaired GluN2B function, we first developed a series of potent and selective GluN2B-containing NMDAR PAMs through virtual high-throughput screening. We then characterized the pharmacological properties of a lead compound, 175, and evaluated its effects on hippocampal synaptic plasticity in anesthetized rats. Furthermore, 175 restored cognitive and behavioral deficits in a Mecp2 overexpression (Mecp2-OE) mouse model with GluN2B hypofunction and a disrupted in schizophrenia 1 (Disc1)–N-terminal fragment (N) transgenic mouse model with similar behavioral abnormalities. This study introduces the first class of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR subtype–selective PAMs and examines their behavioral pharmacology in rodent disease models, bringing to attention the potential of GluN2B-specific PAMs in treating various neuropsychiatric symptoms.

## RESULTS

### Development of potent and selective GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs

Despite the recent development of NMDAR PAMs, including GluN2A-NMDAR–selective PAMs, as therapeutics for central nervous system (CNS) disorders (31–34), no potent, GluN2B-NMDAR–specific PAMs have been reported. We used a computer-assisted, structure-based approach to develop PAMs for GluN2B subunit–containing NMDARs. We virtually screened 1.3 million lead-like compounds on three previously identified subtype-specific, allosteric sites on the extracellular domains of the diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR, the most common form of GluN2B-containing NMDARs (Fig. 1A). These bindings sites include an N-terminal domain (NTD) site for polyamines (site 1) (38), an NTD site known to bind to many GluN2B negative allosteric modulators (NAMs; site 2) (40, 41), and an analogous site in ligand-binding domain (LBD) for GluN2A-specific PAM GNE-6901 (site 3) (35). Among the compounds with top binding scores, we manually inspected their structures and selected a diverse subset of 40 compounds for subsequent in vitro screening, assessing their modulatory effects on whole-cell currents gated through the recombinant, diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR transiently expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells (fig. S1A and table S1). Our in vitro screening identified several NAMs and compound VS20 as the sole PAM of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR (fig. S1A). We then used a structure-activity relationship analysis–based approach to optimize the PAM effect of VS20 (fig. S1B and tables S2 and S3) and developed compounds 170, 175, 182, and 189 as lead molecules with strong efficacy at potentiating diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents (two- to fourfold current potentiation at 1 μM; Fig. 1, B to D).

To determine whether our lead modulators were selective for GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR over other NMDAR subtypes, we transiently expressed the diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A and GluN1/GluN2B-NMDARs on HEK293 cells and measured the dose-dependent modulatory activities of the lead compounds on these two predominant NMDAR subtypes. We found that while all four compounds showed selectivity for modulating GluN2B current (Fig. 1, E to H, and fig. S2), three of four modulators are more potent at potentiating GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents than GluN1/GluN2A-NMDAR currents (170: logEC50 = –6.91 ± 0.14 versus −5.08 ± 0.21, ***P < 0.001; 175: logEC50 = –7.36 ± 0.24 versus −5.61 ± 0.30, **P < 0.01; 182: logEC50 = –7.10 ± 0.20 versus −5.89 ± 0.24, ***P < 0.001; 189: logEC50 = –7.19 ± 0.20 versus −7.47 ± 0.46, P = 0.69; Fig. 1, E to H). By contrast, compound 189 exhibits GluN2B selectivity through increased efficacy (top value: 5.31 ± 0.40 versus 1.63 ± 0.05; **P < 0.01). Moreover, the lead modulator 175 (1 μM) did not affect diheteromeric GluN1/GluN2C- and GluN1/GluN2D-NMDAR currents, but 175 (0.3 and 3 μM) potentiated triheteromeric GluN1/GluN2A/GluN2B-NMDAR currents (fig. S3). Accounting for its superior modulatory efficacy and/or GluN2B selectivity compared with 170 and 182 and higher cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) availability following intraperitoneal (ip) injection in rats compared with 189 (fig. S4), we chose 175 over other lead candidates for further characterization.

### Characterizing PAM175 binding site and pharmacological effects on diheteromeric GluN2B-NMDAR currents

To further understand the structural bases of subtype-dependent, positive allosteric modulation of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents by our PAMs, we characterized the binding site of the lead candidate 175. We first tested 175 on mutant GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR lacking GluN2B-NTD (amino acids 29 to 404) and found that 175 (0.03 to 3 μM) had no effect on the NMDAR current (fig. S5, A and B), confirming that 175 binds to the NTD of the receptor. Our initial virtual screening hit compound VS20 had the highest binding score to the phenylethanolamine binding site among the known NTD allosteric binding sites of the GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR (40). Thus, we performed docking of 175 on this site to model its detailed binding poses. Our structural model predicted that 175 had overlapping but distinct binding poses compared with GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR NAM Ro25-6981 (Fig. 2A). To experimentally validate our structural model, we performed site-directed mutagenesis on amino acid residues surrounding the putative binding site. We chose GluN1 L135, GluN2B Q110, and GluN2B F114 residues for mutagenesis based on their previously determined interactions with GluN2B-containing NMDAR NAM Ro25-6981 (40). We found that GluN2B Q110A and GluN2B F114S mutations, but not GluN1 L135Q mutation, reduced the efficacy and/or potency of 175 on modulating GluN2B-NMDAR currents (Fig. 2B). Our results suggest that 175 (and other PAMs in this group) binds to an overlapping site with Ro25-6981 by interacting with Q110 and F114 on the GluN2B but differs from Ro25-6981 by not interacting with L135 on the GluN1. Computational modeling of the binding pose confirms these interactions and revealed potential interaction of 175 with D113 (2B), A135 (2B), T105 (N1), and I133 (N1) (fig. S5C). The unique binding pose of 175 compared with GluN2B antagonists including Ro25-6981 and EVT-001 may be critical for its positive rather than negative allosteric modulation on GluN2B-NMDAR.

Different modes of positive allosteric modulation of NMDAR currents may result in distinct physiological consequences (35, 36). NMDAR PAMs are primarily categorized into type I PAMs, which enhance the maximal channel current in the presence of agonist (glutamate) without affecting the glutamate potency, and type II PAMs, which enhance the glutamate potency without affecting the maximal channel current (36). To determine the mode of positive allosteric modulation by 175, we measured the glutamate dose response (0.01 to 100 μM) on activating GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents with and without 175 (1 μM) in the bath solution (Fig. 2, C and D). 175 resulted in an upward shift of the glutamate dose-response curve without enhancing the glutamate potency (Fig. 2D). We also determined whether the PAM effect of 175 was dependent on glutamate concentration. In contrast to many of the existing NMDAR PAMs but similar to polyamines and ifenprodil (35, 42, 43), the efficacy of 175 on modulating GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents was much higher when the glutamate concentration was 100 μM versus when the glutamate concentration was 1 μM (Fig. 2, E and F). This characteristic of 175 may allow it to preferentially potentiate NMDARs activated by high micromolar to millimolar glutamate concentration (typically during synaptic vesicle release) but less by the submicromolar concentration of ambient glutamate (44). By contrast, the positive modulatory efficacy of 175 remains the same whether the concentration of glycine is at 30 or 0.1 μM (fig. S6).

### GluN2B-subunit–specific positive modulation of native NMDAR currents in cultured neurons by compound 175

Unlike recombinant GluN1/GluN2B-NMDARs, native NMDARs expressed on neurons have a higher level of subtype diversity and a larger number of postsynaptic interacting proteins, and, consequently, may exhibit different receptor pharmacology (13). We, therefore, investigated whether 175 could modulate native NMDAR-gated currents in a GluN2B-containing subtype–specific manner in neurons (Fig. 1A). Using primary neurons in culture between 9 and 11 days in vitro (DIV), a time when the GluN2B subunit expression was predominant, we first tested how 175 modulated the neuronal NMDAR currents induced by aspartate (100 μM for 0.5 s), an agonist specific for the NMDA-type glutamate receptors (45). Consistent with the results from GluN2B-NMDAR current recordings in HEK293 cells, we observed a dose-dependent potentiation of neuronal NMDAR currents by 175 (0.0001 to 1 μM; Fig. 3, A and B). The maximal current potentiation (5.53- ± 1.52-fold at 1 μM) and logEC50 (−7.74 ± 0.15) of 175 were comparable to those observed for recombinant GluN1/GluN2B-NMDARs (5.14- ± 0.56-fold at 1 μM and logEC50 = −7.36 ± 0.24). Our results demonstrate that 175 effectively potentiates neuronal NMDAR currents measured during a developmental time point when GluN2B-containing NMDAR expression likely predominates other NMDAR subtypes.

To further investigate whether the positive modulatory effect of 175 on NMDAR currents is GluN2B-subtype dependent in neurons, we used subtype-dependent inhibitors of NMDARs to isolate different components of the NMDAR-gated currents. We first use a GluN2A preferential antagonist NVP (0.2 μM), which was reported to block nearly all GluN2A component of NMDAR currents at this concentration, albeit also with a minor contaminant blockade of the GluN2B component of NMDAR currents (46). The remaining non-GluN2A component could still be potentiated by 175 (Fig. 3, C and D). We then used Ro25-6981 to block the GluN2B component of NMDAR currents, and we found that the remaining non-GluN2B component was no longer potentiated by 175 (Fig. 3, E and F). Together, our evidence supported that 175, at the concentration used in this experiment (0.1 μM), specifically potentiated GluN2B-subunit (but not GluN2A-subunit)–containing NMDAR currents in cultured neurons.

We also investigated whether 175 had off-target effects on other major ion channels. γ-Aminobutyric acid type A receptors (GABAARs) and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) are principal ligand-gated ion channels mediating fast inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmissions, respectively. We found that at its saturating concentration for modulating GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents (1 μM), 175 slightly potentiated GABAAR currents evoked by GABA (10 μM), resulting in a 1.17- ± 0.06-fold change in currents (Fig. 3, G and H), which was more than an order of magnitude lower than its efficacy on modulating NMDAR currents (5.53- ± 1.52-fold; Fig. 3, A and B) in neurons. We then conducted a dose-response measurement of 175 (0.01 to 100 μM) on modulating GABAAR currents but did not detect any current potentiation (fig. S7, A and B). The dose-response experiments required longer recordings and were affected by GABAAR current desensitization and, therefore, had lower sensitivity than the single-dose application of 175 at 1 μM for detecting small current potentiation. Moreover, 175 did not affect AMPAR-mediated currents evoked by AMPA (30 μM; Fig. 3, I and J) or currents gated by voltage-gated sodium channels and voltage-gated potassium channels (fig. S7, C to F). Overall, at its saturating concentration for modulating GluN2B-NMDAR currents, 175 had mild PAM effects on GABAARs and had no effects on AMPAR, voltage-gated sodium channels, and voltage-gated potassium channels in neurons.

Overactivation of GluN2B-NMDARs is thought to induce neuronal excitotoxicity (47, 48). To assess the neurotoxic liability of potentiating GluN2B-NMDARs, we treated the neurons with 175 (1 μM for 3 hours) and measured cell viability using a Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay. Treatment with 175 did not affect cell viability relative to vehicle (Veh; fig. S8).

### GluN2B-NMDAR PAM 175 facilitates hippocampal synaptic plasticity in vivo

NMDARs have been recognized as the principal ion channels mediating the induction of hippocampal CA1 long-term potentiation (LTP) and LTD, two best-characterized forms of synaptic plasticity (49, 50). Transgenic mice lacking the GluN2B subunit have impaired synaptic plasticity, especially LTD (4, 16, 20). By contrast, enhancing NMDAR functions by overexpressing GluN2B in transgenic mice or using pharmacological agents facilitates synaptic plasticity (22, 51). We hypothesized that our PAMs, by positively modulating GluN2B-containing NMDAR functions, would modulate long-term synaptic plasticity in rats. To examine the in vivo effects of 175 on hippocampal synaptic plasticity, we first determined the plasma and CSF availability of 175 after intraperitoneal injections (5 mg/kg) in rats. We collected serum and CSF samples at various time points postinjection (15, 30, 120, and 240 min) and used mass spectrometry to estimate the free/unbound 175 concentrations. We found that 175 was rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream (46.09 ± 12.06 μM at 15 min) and a fraction (~6%) of the plasma concentration was detected in the CSF (fig. S4A). By contrast, the fraction of another lead candidate 189 detected in the CSF was extremely low (<0.1%; fig. S4B). Given that the unbound 175 concentrations in CSF (0.78 ± 0.27 μM at 120 min) were more than an order of magnitude higher than its median effective concentration (EC50; 0.04 μM) on modulating GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR currents, the concentration of 175 that reached the target GluN2B-containing NMDARs was likely sufficient to induce a long-lasting (>2 hours) positive modulatory effect.

On the basis of the pharmacokinetics data of 175 (fig. S4A), we used 175 (1 mg/kg) intraperitoneal injections 30 min before the induction of synaptic plasticity for subsequent in vivo experiments. To determine the effects of 175 on hippocampal synaptic plasticity, we measured the evoked field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP) in the Schaffer collateral to CA1 pathway of the dorsal hippocampus in anesthetized rats. First, we used high-frequency stimulation (HFS) to induce NMDAR-dependent forms of LTP. We found that compared with Veh treatment, 175 injections slightly increased the late phase of a weak, decaying form of LTP induced by one train of HFS (100 Hz for 1 s; Fig. 4, A and B) but had no effect on a strong, saturated form of LTP induced by four trains of HFS (Fig. 4, C and D). These results are consistent with the previous findings that activation of GluN2B-containing NMDAR only has mild, context-dependent effects on the induction of hippocampal LTP (4, 16, 52). We next investigated how 175 affected LTD induced by low-frequency stimulation (LFS; 1 Hz for 900 s). We found that in the absence of 175, LFS failed to produce noticeable LTD (Fig. 4, E and F), consistent with previous studies showing that LTD was difficult to induce in adult rats (53, 54). However, in rats pretreated with 175, LFS robustly produced LTD (Fig. 4, E and F), suggesting that 175 treatments facilitated the induction of LTD. To determine whether this LTD facilitation effect was mediated by 175 acting on GluN2B-containing NMDARs, we coinjected 175 with a GluN2B-containing NMDAR antagonist Ro25-6981 (10 mg/kg, ip). We found that Ro25-6981 coinjection abolished the LTD facilitation effect of 175 (Fig. 4, E and F). Our results support that 175 facilitates the dorsal hippocampal LTD via a GluN2B-containing NMDAR–dependent mechanism in vivo and is consistent with the previously reported roles of GluN2B-containing NMDARs in LTD (4, 14, 16, 20).

### Enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR function reversed behavioral abnormalities in open-field and three-chamber tests in Mecp2-OE mice

Overexpression of Mecp2 is a mouse model of MECP2 duplication syndrome in humans, which leads to the development of autistic-like features, including increased anxiety and mental retardation, in patients (55). Given that Mecp2-OE mice develop a set of neuropsychiatric phenotypes that resembles mice with GluN2B loss of function (55–57), we reasoned that Mecp2 mice are a suitable model upon which the treatment efficacy of our GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs can be tested. First, we performed immunoblot experiments on the cortical/hippocampal lysates from 9-month-old Mecp2-OE mice. We observed reduced GluN2B (but not GluN2A) expression in the hippocampus of Mecp2-OE mice compared with WT controls (fig. S9, A to C). This result contrasts with the increased GluN2B expression in Mecp2 null mice and is consistent with the MECP2’s role in epigenetic regulation of GluN2B expression (58, 59).

We then conducted a battery of behavioral assays on Mecp2-OE and Mecp2 WT mice treated with 175 (1 mg/kg, ip) or Veh 30 min before each behavioral test (Fig. 5A). Behavioral assays were performed at both 3 and 7 months of age, as a previous study reported age-dependent, progressive behavioral deficits in this mouse model (57). The open-field test is commonly used to assess locomotion and anxiety-like behaviors in mouse models of neuropsychiatric diseases, and it is also valuable for examining the side effects of modulators targeting NMDARs (Fig. 5B). Compared with WT mice, Mecp2-OE mice had normal locomotion and center time in the open-field test at 3 months (Fig. 5, C and D) but increased locomotion and decreased center time at 7 months (Fig. 5, E and F). At 7 months, while the 175 treatment did not affect locomotion, it restored center time in Mecp2-OE mice to WT levels (Fig. 5, E and F), indicating a reversal of anxiety-like behavior. 175 treatments (1 mg/kg) did not affect the distance traveled in Mecp2 WT mice (Fig. 5, C and E) and in WT rats during a 1-hour-long open-field test (fig. S10), suggesting that 175 injections did not induce any locomotor-related side effects.

Next, we evaluate the explorative behaviors in Mecp2-OE mice and Mecp2 WT controls using a Y-maze task (fig. S9D) (60). At 3 months, Mecp2-OE mice exhibited normal exploration compared to WT controls, but at 7 months, their exploratory behavior was impaired, as indicated by fewer entries into the novel arm (fig. S9, E and F). Following the 175 treatment, Mecp2-OE mice showed an increase in entries (12.57 ± 1.81 versus 9.17 ± 1.80), although this was not statistically different from the Mecp2-OE + Veh group (fig. S9F).

We then performed a three-chamber test to assess sociability and social cognition for WT and Mecp2-OE mice at 7 months (Fig. 5,G to L). During the first phase, the test animal was allowed to interact with a mouse or an empty cage. Sociability was assessed by quantifying the time spent in each chamber and social preference indexes (see Fig. 5G and Materials and Methods). WT, but not Mecp2-OE, mice (treated with Veh) showed a preference for the mouse (M1) over object (O), indicating reduced sociability of Mecp2-OE mice at 7 months (Fig. 5, H and I). Following the 175 treatment, the social preference index in Mecp2-OE mice was mildly improved (0.12 ± 0.12 versus −0.08 ± 0.25) but did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 5I). During the second phase, test animals were allowed to interact with a familiar (M1) or a novel mouse (M2; Fig. 5J). Mecp2-OE mice treated with Veh exhibited a strong trend toward impaired social cognition compared with WT mice, based on the preference index (Fig. 5, K and L). Moreover, treatment with 175 significantly improved the preference index in Mecp2-OE mice compared to Veh-treated Mecp2-OE mice (Fig. 5L), suggesting that 175 reversed social cognition deficits in Mecp2-OE mice. 175 treatment also slightly increased the preference index in WT mice (0.34 + 0.08 for WT + 175 versus 0.22 + 0.09 for WT + Veh), but the change was not statistically significant. Overall, our data support that enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR function with 175 reverses anxiety-like behaviors and social cognition deficits, which are characteristic phenotypes of the Mecp2-OE mouse model (57).

### GluN2B-NMDAR PAM rescued behavioral impairments in open-field, Y-maze spontaneous alternation, three-chamber test, and prepulse inhibition in Disc1-N mice

Pathogenic mutations in the DISC1 gene in humans increase the risk of developing neuropsychiatric diseases (61). To demonstrate that our GluN2B-selective NMDAR PAMs might reverse GluN2B-dependent cognitive and behavioral symptoms in another mouse model of neurodevelopmental disorders, we administrated drug 175 in a transgenic mouse line harboring an inducible expression of Disc1-N mice. Disc1 transgenic mouse models had abnormal DISC1 protein functions and altered synaptic functions, including abnormal NMDAR currents and impaired LTD (62, 63), along with a broad range of behavioral deficits, including increased anxiety and impaired behavioral flexibility (11, 61, 62, 64). Tamoxifen (or oil) injections were administered intraperitoneally every 2 days to both Disc1-N mice and Disc1 WT littermates, starting at 1 to 2 months of age, to induce transgene expression only in Disc1-N mice receiving tamoxifen. The animals underwent behavioral tests at 3 to 4 months of age (Fig. 6A).

We first investigated locomotion and anxiety-like behaviors in Disc1 WT and Disc1-N mice using an open-field test (Fig. 6B). During the 10-min testing period, Disc1-N mice treated with tamoxifen (Disc1-TAM) traveled shorter distances than those receiving oil (Disc1-OIL) (Fig. 6C). Moreover, Disc1-TAM animals spent less time in the center of the open field compared with Disc1-OIL, WT-OIL, and WT-TAM mice, suggesting increased anxiety-like behavior in Disc1-N mice (Fig. 6D). To assess the effects of compound 175, we injected Disc1-TAM mice with 175 (1 mg/kg, ip) or Veh 20 min before testing. While 175 did not alter locomotion, it significantly increased the time spent in the center (Fig. 6, E and F). Together, our data suggest that 175 reduces anxiety-like behavior in Disc1-N mice in an open-field test without affecting distances traveled.

Next, we examined whether Disc1-N mice had impaired performance in Y-maze spontaneous alternation, a task for assessing spatial working memory and executive function (Fig. 6G) (60). Disc1-TAM mice had reduced spontaneous alternation compared with Disc1-OIL, WT-OIL, and WT-TAM mice, whereas the total entry to the arms was not significantly different among the groups (Fig. 6, H and I). We then treated Disc1-TAM mice with 175 or Veh. Compared with the mice that received Veh treatment, Disc1-TAM mice receiving 175 had increased spontaneous alternation (Fig. 6, J and K). Our evidence suggests that GluN2B-NMDAR PAM 175 reverses the spatial working memory deficit in Disc1-N mice during Y-maze spontaneous alternation.

Given that 175 ameliorated sociability and social cognition deficits in Mecp2-OE mice, we wondered whether similar prosocial effects would be observed in Disc1-N mice. We performed a three-chamber test to assess sociability (Fig. 6L). Disc1-TAM mice had a reduced social preference index compared with Disc1-OIL, WT-OIL, and WT-TAM mice (Fig. 6M). Administration of 175 (1 mg/kg) increased the social preference index of Disc1-TAM mice compared with Veh treatment (Fig. 6N), while the total distance traveled by mice in each group was not significantly different (fig. S11), suggesting that 175 treatment reversed abnormal sociability in Disc1-N mice.

Abnormal sensory processing is a common symptom in patients with neuropsychiatric disorders and has been linked to GluN2B-dependent LTD (65, 66). We used an acoustic startle paradigm to measure the prepulse inhibition (PPI) of the startle response to the auditory stimuli (Fig. 6O), which refers to the ability of a weak prestimulus to transiently suppress the response to a subsequent strong stimulus and is widely used for assessing abnormal sensorimotor gating (11, 65). We found that all groups of mice had reduced startle response when a weaker auditory stimulus with various intensities (71, 76, or 81 dB) preceded a strong auditory stimulus (120 dB) and had similar baseline startle responses to the 120-dB auditory stimulus (Fig. 6P); however, the magnitude of PPI was significantly smaller in Disc1-TAM mice compared with mice in any other groups (Fig. 6, Q to S). Furthermore, compared with Disc1-TAM mice receiving Veh injection, those receiving 175 (1 mg/kg) had unchanged baseline startle response but increased PPI when the prepulse intensity was 71, 76, or 81 dB (Fig. 6, T to W). Together, our data support that drug 175 rescues multiple behavioral abnormalities in Disc1-N mice that are commonly observed in mouse models of neurodevelopmental disorders.

## DISCUSSION

NMDAR PAMs have been in clinical trials for cognitive symptoms in neurological diseases (31, 32). However, there is a lack of subtype-specific PAMs targeting GluN2B-containing NMDARs, and the therapeutic benefits of enhancing GluN2B-containing NMDAR functions are unknown. In this study, we developed PAMs targeting the GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR, including compound 175 with 0.044 μM potency on GluN2B-NMDAR, which is ~56-fold more potent than on GluN1/GluN2A-NMDAR. Moreover, the GluN2B selectivity of compound 175 is further enhanced by having a better efficacy at potentiating GluN2B- than GluN2A-NMDAR. We characterized the drug binding site and the specificity of 175 against other major classes of ion channels. Furthermore, we validated the use of the lead drug 175 in vivo by assessing its availability in CSF and its effect on GluN2B-NMDAR–dependent synaptic plasticity in rats.

Using two genetic mouse models (Mecp2-OE and Disc1-N mice) that mimicked the symptoms (anxiety-like behaviors, impaired social function, spatial working memory, PPI, etc.) and the critical pathophysiology (hypofunction of GluN2B-NMDAR and/or impaired synaptic plasticity) in neuropsychiatric diseases, we found that our lead GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR PAM 175 reversed many cognitive and behavioral deficits in both mouse models. This evidence underscores the importance of NMDAR hypofunction in neurodevelopmental disorders and demonstrates the therapeutic potential of GluN2B-NMDAR–specific PAMs for treating various neuropsychiatric symptoms associated with GluN2B-NMDAR hypofunction.

### The utility of GluN2B-specific NMDAR PAMs

Developing NMDAR PAMs with subtype specificity, including those specific for the GluN2B-containing subtypes, has been a longstanding challenge (30). Our study addresses this hurdle by developing potent, selective, and in vivo–ready GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs, parallel to what has been done for GluN2A- and GluN2C/D-containing NMDARs by other research groups (33, 35, 66, 67). Moreover, by characterizing the binding site of our GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs, we provide evidence that subtype-specific positive modulation can occur at an NTD binding site overlapping with those of commonly used GluN2B-NMDAR antagonists (40, 68). This finding aligns with studies demonstrating the NTD’s structural roles in bidirectional gating of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDARs (69–71). The bidirectional allosteric modulations of NMDARs by drugs have also been reported for several other non-NTD allosteric sites on NMDARs (35, 72, 73). Our research expands the landscape of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR pharmacology and provides a foundation for developing structurally diverse, subtype-specific PAMs with desired pharmacological properties.

The PAMs for GluN2B-containing NMDARs will serve as valuable tools for investigating the functional diversity of NMDAR subunits. Although numerous studies have explored the roles of different NMDAR subunits in various physiological functions, including synaptic plasticity and neuronal fate, the precise contribution of each NMDAR subtype to those physiological functions remains unclear (13, 14). Our potent and subunit-specific GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs can be used in conjunction with the recently developed GluN2A-NMDAR PAMs to understand the roles of NMDAR subtypes in synaptic plasticity and learning, an area of research that has been hampered by controversial results (52, 74). Moreover, the unique glutamate-concentration dependency of our lead compound 175, which requires an above EC50 level of glutamate concentration for optimal PAM efficacy, may allow us to preferentially target GluN2B-containing NMDARs when the glutamate concentration is high and minimal potentiate the tonic activation of GluN2B-containing NMDARs.

Clinical development of NMDAR-targeting drugs, including NMDAR agonists and antagonists, has been hindered by substantial on-target side effects stemming from the widespread expression of these receptors throughout the CNS (10, 75). By developing allosteric modulators targeting GluN2B-containing NMDARs with preferential efficacy at an above EC50 level of glutamate concentration on GluN2B-NMDARs, the side effects associated with NMDAR modulation may be minimized. Locomotion-related impairment in mice has been reported after treatment with GluN2A-targeting PAMs (33), and acute injections with our GluN2B-NMDAR PAM, compound 175, did not affect locomotor activity in multiple rodent species and genotypes. Nevertheless, because GluN2B-NMDAR overactivation is known to contribute to excitotoxicity, particularly under pathological conditions such as stroke (76, 77), the use of these modulators should be approached with caution in neurotoxic or neurodegenerative settings. Our CCK-8 assay in cultured neurons suggests that 175 does not induce cytotoxicity at a concentration that maximally potentiates GluN2B-NMDAR (1 μM). However, the on-target toxicity of potentiating GluN2B warrant further investigations using various in vitro and in vivo assays.

### Behavioral pharmacology of GluN2B-containing NMDAR PAMs

Loss of the GluN2B subunit in mice has consistently been linked to impaired LTD and learning, especially learning that requires flexible adaptation to changing situations (14, 21). Multiple independently generated mouse strains with conditional knockout of the GluN2B subunit have impairments in working memory–like tasks such as T-maze spontaneously alternation (16, 21). In our experiment, we found that 175 treatments reversed impaired Y-maze spontaneously alternation in Disc1-N mice, consistent with the roles of GluN2B in spatial working memory. These findings demonstrate that 175 reversed a GluN2B-dependent cognitive function and established the basis for further exploring its therapeutic benefits in a broader range of GluN2B- and/or LTD-dependent learning deficits, such as impaired reversal learning and fear extinction, in animal models.

Although NMDAR PAMs have various effects on anxiety-like behaviors, the precise role of NMDAR activation on anxiety is unknown and is likely dependent on receptor subtypes being targeted (33, 78). We demonstrated that GluN2B-NMDAR PAM reversed anxiety-like behaviors in the open-field test in Mecp2-OE and Disc1-N mice. Our study suggests the potential of 175 in alleviating anxiety, but it is important to further evaluate its effects using a broad range of behavioral tasks for anxiety and to compare with drugs such as GluN2A-NMDAR PAMs to further understand the roles of enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR function in anxiety. While some studies using Disc1 transgenic mice observed anxiety-like behaviors (62), others reported opposite phenotypes, such as hyperlocomotion and increased risk-taking behaviors (61, 64). Although a coherent phenotype has not been established across research groups—likely due to variations in transgenic lines, behavioral protocols, and tamoxifen injection regimens—our Disc1-N mice consistently exhibit an anxiety-like phenotype, making them a reliable model for testing the therapeutic potential of 175.

Impaired social function is a defining symptom of ASD in humans and a key symptom in many other neuropsychiatric disorders (55, 79). Transgenic mice with the GluN2B subunit replaced by GluN2A display impaired social exploratory behaviors in three-chamber tests (15). Moreover, impaired social behavior in Shank2 mutant mice, which also had reduced NMDAR function, is restored by improving NMDAR function using d-cycloserine (18). Consistent with the critical role of GluN2B hypofunction in impaired social function, we showed that enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR function with 175 reversed sociability deficit in Disc1-N mice and social cognition deficit in Mecp2-OE mice, highlighting the potential of the drug in restoring impaired social function in neurodevelopmental diseases.

Impaired sensorimotor gating and abnormal salience to less relevant environmental stimuli have been implicated in neuropsychiatric diseases, especially schizophrenia (80, 81). These symptoms have been associated with the impaired ability of the brain to filter out irrelevant information, a process that may be dependent on LTD (29, 80). Our study shows that enhancing GluN2B-NMDAR reversed PPI deficits in Disc1-N mice. Similar effects have also been reported by PAMs targeting the GluN2C/GluN2D subunits. Hence, the potential and precise roles of targeting different NMDAR subunits in improving sensorimotor gating deficits warrant further investigation.

### Therapeutic potential of GluN2B-containing NMDAR PAMs

Hypofunction of GluN2B has been robustly associated with ASD and neurodevelopmental delay in humans (3). In addition, reduced activity of NMDARs is a critical mechanism in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia and age-dependent cognitive decline (14, 18, 82). Impaired synaptic plasticity has been associated with cognitive disabilities in neurodegenerative diseases, intellectual disabilities, and mood disorders (14, 83, 84). Recently, PAMs targeting NMDARs have been investigated in phase 2 clinical trials for several of these conditions, highlighting the wide-ranging therapeutic potential of these drugs (31, 32). The development of GluN2B-specific PAM provides an additional, more targeted approach and a worth-exploring opportunity for treating these neuropsychiatric diseases.

### Virtual screening of allosteric modulators targeting GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR

Virtual screening of compounds targeting GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR was conducted using a chemical library containing 1.3 million small-molecule, drug-like compounds (ChemBridge Corporation). Docking was performed on three known binding sites located at the NTD or LBD of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR (35, 38, 40) using an open-source software AutoDock Vina (Scripps Research Institute). The active-state structure of GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR (Protein Data Bank ID: 5FXG) was used as the docking template. The center coordinates for the three binding sites were set to [167, 148, 132] for site 1, [172, 133, 112] for site 2, and [149, 155, 166] for site 3. For each site, the search space was defined as a cubic box with dimensions of 20 Å by 20 Å by 20 Å. AutoDock Vina was run with an exhaustiveness parameter of 8 and the number of output poses of 1.

The best 1000 compounds (~0.1% of the library) and their binding poses were visualized using PyMOL (Schrodinger). These molecules were visually inspected for chemical diversity, drug-likeness, CNS-relevant absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties, and commercial availability. Compounds with potentially reactive substructures, predicted toxicity, poor solubility, extreme logP values, or lack of commercial availability were subjectively excluded by an experienced medicinal chemist. The top 40 compounds were purchased for experimental screening of their modulatory activities on GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR.

### HEK293 cell culture and plasmid transfection

HEK293 (American Type Culture Collection, CRL-1573) cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and were maintained in a cell culture incubator at 37°C with 5% CO2. For transient expression of the NMDAR subunits, cells were grown to 70 to 90% confluency in six-well plates and were cotransfected with the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP)–GluN1/GluN2A (1 μg:1 μg), the EGFP-GluN1/GluN2B (1 μg:1 μg), or the EGFP-GluN1-3xATG/GluN2A-C1/GluN2B-C2 (1 μg:0.5 μg:0.5 μg) plasmids. Transfections were performed using the Lipofectamine 2000 reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After the transfection, cells were maintained in six-well plates for another 5 hours before being replated onto 12-mm glass coverslips coated with poly-l-lysine (Sigma-Aldrich). An NMDAR antagonist d-APV (100 μM; Hello Bio) was added to the cell culture medium to improve cell viability, and the transfected cells were cultured for an additional 18 to 30 hours before electrophysiology experiments.

### Drug preparation

All screening and lead GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR PAMs were first dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to a concentration of 100 mM and then diluted into the extracellular recording solution (ECS) to their testing concentrations (0.001 to 100 μM). For in vivo administration, 175 (Enamine) was first dissolved in DMSO (100 mM) and then diluted in saline to a final concentration of 2 or 10 mg/ml, and a final concentration of 1 to 5 mg/kg was used during intraperitoneal injection depending on the experiments. Ro25-6981 maleate (Alomone Labs) was dissolved in saline to 4 mg/ml, and 6 mg/kg was used for intraperitoneal injection. Tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich) was dissolved in corn oil (0.01 g/ml; Meryer), and 50 mg/kg was used for intraperitoneal injection.

### Site-directed mutagenesis

Site-directed mutagenesis was performed using plasmids encoding the GluN1 or GluN2B subunit as the template. Forward primers containing 21 base pairs (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were designed for each mutation, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–mediated site-directed mutagenesis was performed with a high-fidelity DNA polymerase (KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix, Cedarlane). For the digestion of the original plasmids, DpnI (1 μl; New England Biolabs) was added to the PCR product and incubated at 37°C for 30 min. The product was then transformed into DH5α competent cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for selection and plasmid preparation, and the sequences of the mutated plasmids were confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Azenta Inc.).

### Primary culture of rat hippocampal neurons

Dissociated cultures of rat hippocampal neurons were prepared from both male and female embryonic day 18 Sprague-Dawley rats (Charles River Laboratories) and were maintained in Neurobasal medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing the B-27 supplement (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were plated onto 24-well plates with 12-mm coverslips, and electrophysiology recordings were conducted once the cells reached DIV 9 to 14.

### Patch-clamp electrophysiology

Whole-cell voltage-clamp electrophysiology recordings of HEK293 cells and neurons were performed at room temperature as previously described (85). The signals were low-pass filtered at 2 kHz using a MultiClamp 700A amplifier (Molecular Devices) and digitized at 10 kHz using Digidata 1322A (Molecular Devices). The standard ECS was Mg2+ free and contained 140 mM NaCl, 5.4 mM KCl, 1.3 mM CaCl2, 25 mM Hepes, and 33 mM glucose (pH = 7.4; 310 to 320 mosmol). During recordings, the patch pipettes were filled with an internal solution containing 130 mM CsMeSO3, 8 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM Hepes, 0.5 mM EGTA, and 4 mM adenosine 5′-triphosphate (ATP) (K) (pH = 7.2; 290 to 300 mosmol). A CsCl-based intracellular solution containing 135 mM CsCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM CaCl2, 10 mM 1,2-bis(2-aminophenoxy)ethane-N,N,N′tN′-tetraacetic acid, 10 mM Hepes, and 4 mM ATP (K) (pH = 7.2; 290 to 300 mosmol) was used for the recordings of GABAAR currents.

For compound screening on GluN1/GluN2B-NMDAR, 1 μM glycine was added to the Mg2+-free ECS while maintaining a holding voltage of –60 mV. NMDAR-gated currents were induced by applying ECS containing 10 μM glutamate for 3 s, using an SF-77B two-barrel fast-step perfusion system (Harvard Apparatus). The screening compounds were included in both the bath solution and the glutamate-containing solution to determine their modulatory effects on NMDAR currents. For lead compound characterization and dose-response experiments, 30 μM glycine was added to the Mg2+-free ECS, and NMDAR currents were induced by applying ECS containing 100 μM glutamate for 2 s.

For drug dose-response experiments on neuronal NMDARs, primary cultures of hippocampal neurons (DIV 9 to10) were used while maintaining a holding voltage of –60 mV. MgCl2 (1 mM), glycine (1 μM), and strychnine (1 μM) were added to the ECS. We used 1 mM MgCl2 to mimic physiological conditions and partially block NMDAR currents, thereby enabling stable recordings over extended periods. A brief pulse of d-, l-aspartate (100 μM for 0.5 s) was used to induce NMDAR-gated currents, and 175 was introduced into the bath solution at various concentrations (from 0.0001 to 1 μM) to examine its modulatory effect on neuronal NMDAR currents.

To investigate the subtype specificity of the PAMs on modulating neuronal NMDAR currents, primary cultures of hippocampal neurons (DIV 12 to 14) were used with the holding voltage maintained at –40 mV. MgCl2 (1 mM), glycine (1 μM), and strychnine (1 μM) were added to the ECS. A brief pulse of d-, l-aspartate (100 μM for 0.5 s) was used to induce NMDAR-gated currents, and NVP (0.2 μM) and Ro25-6981 (10 μM) were added to the bath solution to block the GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDAR currents, respectively. Subsequently, 175 (0.1 μM) was added to the bath solution to assess its modulatory effects on the unblocked portion of the neuronal NMDAR currents.

To record AMPAR currents in neurons, patch-clamp electrophysiology on hippocampal neurons (DIV 12 to 14) was conducted with a holding voltage maintained at –60 mV. MgCl2 (2 mM) was added to the ECS. AMPA (30 μM for 0.5 s) was applied to induce the AMPAR currents, and a high concentration of 175 (1 μM) was added to examine its modulatory effect on AMPAR currents. To record GABAAR currents in neurons, the CsCl-based intracellular solution was used in the recording pipette, and MgCl2 (2 mM) was added to the ECS. GABA (10 μM for 2 s) was applied briefly to induce GABAAR-gated currents, while the cells were maintained at a holding voltage of –60 mV. 175 (1 μM) was added to examine its modulatory effect on GABAAR currents. To record the dose response of 175 on GABAAR-gated currents, GABA (10 μM for 1 s) was applied to induce GABAAR-gated currents and then incrementally increased the concentration of 175 (0.01 to 100 μM) in the bath solution.

### CCK-8 cytotoxicity assay

Primary cortical neurons were prepared from both male and female neonatal C57BL/6 mice (Charles River Laboratories) and plated in 96-well plates. At DIV 14, cells were exposed for 3 hours to one of the following conditions: untreated (negative control), Veh control, 1 μM compound 175, or 1% Triton X-100 (positive control), all prepared in our standard artificial CSF containing 125 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 2 mM CaCl2, 1.25 mM KH2PO4, 26 mM NaHCO3, and 20 mM glucose. Following treatment, 10 μl of CCK-8 reagent (Beyotime, #C0041) was added directly to each well and incubated for either 30 or 60 min at 37°C. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader, and values were used to quantify cell viability and cytotoxicity relative to controls.

### Pharmacokinetics experiments

Rats received an intraperitoneal injection of 175 or 189 at a dose of 5 mg/kg and CSF, and serum samples were collected at multiple time points (15, 30, 120, and 240 min) following injection to explore the pharmacokinetics of the drug. For CSF and serum collections, rats were anesthetized with urethane (1000 mg/kg, ip). The soft dura of the cisterna magna was exposed following surgical incision, and a 28-gauge 1.27-cm-long insulin syringe was inserted carefully through the dura and aspirated CSF until ~100 μl of fluid is collected. Afterward, ~500 μl of serum was collected from the tail vein using a 28-gauge 1.27-cm-long syringe. Collected CSF samples were immediately put on dry ice, and the serum samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 9000 rpm, after which the plasma layer was collected for further analysis. The drug 175 or 189 in CSF and plasma samples was quantified using mass spectrometry based on a serially diluted standard (175 or 189) in blank CSF or plasma samples, with a structurally similar drug as an internal control.

### In vivo electrophysiology recordings of hippocampal synaptic plasticity

In vivo recordings of synaptic plasticity in the dorsal hippocampus were conducted as previously described (86). Six- to 8-week-old Sprague-Dawley rats are injected with urethane (1000 mg/kg, ip) until reaching the surgical plane of anesthesia. Using stereotaxic surgery techniques, two holes are drilled with coordinates (−3.3 AP, −2.0 ML and − 3.3 AP, −3.0 DV from bregma). A bipolar iridium/platinum stimulating electrode and a unipolar iridium/platinum recording electrode were gently lowered into their respective coordinates (−3.3 AP, −3.0 ML, and ~−2.7 DV and −3.3 AP, −2.0 ML, and ~−2.5 DV from bregma) and were carefully adjusted until reaching a maximal fEPSP response.

Once the electrodes were placed, a 15-min waiting period was introduced for the tissues surrounding the electrodes to recover. For baseline recordings, fEPSPs were induced at 30-s intervals by 0.1-ms stimulations. The stimulation intensity was adjusted so that the signal reached 40% of the maximal fEPSP slope during LTP experiments and 60% of the maximal fEPSP slope during LTD experiments. At least 10 min of stable baseline recordings were obtained before intraperitoneal injection of the treatment drug (175, saline, or 175 + Ro25-6981). Following the drug injections, the baseline recordings were collected for another 20 min before inducing LTP or LTD. LTP was induced using either a strong HFS protocol (4 × 100 Hz for 1 s with 1-min interval) or a weak HFS protocol (1 × 100 Hz for 1 s). LTD was induced using a standard LFS protocol (1 Hz for 900 s). Following the electrical stimulations, the fEPSP signals were collected at 30-s intervals for at least 90 min for LTP and 105 min for LTD experiments.

### Western blotting

Hippocampal brain tissue was manually dissected and lysed on ice in a radioimmunoprecipitation assay lysis buffer (Beyotime, P0013B; contains 50 mM tris, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, sodium orthovanadate, sodium fluoride, EDTA, and leupeptin) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Beyotime, P1005). The lysate was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected for protein concentration analysis using a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of proteins were mixed with 4× sample buffer, boiled at 100°C for 5 min, and subjected to 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Proteins were then transferred to a polyvinylidene difluoride membrane (Bio-Rad) in a wet chamber (110 V for 60 min).

Membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST for 1 hour at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies: rabbit anti-NMDAR2A (ABclonal, A13863; 165 kDa), rabbit anti-NMDAR2B (Abcam, ab254356; 166 kDa), and mouse glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) Polyclonal antibody (Proteintech, HRP-60004; 36 kDa). After washing in TBST (3 × 5 min), membranes were incubated with anti-rabbit horseradish peroxidase (HRP) or anti-mouse HRP (1:10,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1 hour at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using a Bio-Rad Imager, and band densities were quantified the ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health).

### Behavioral experiments

Before testing, all mice (Mecp2-OE, Disc1-N, or their respective WT littermates) were handled and habituated in the testing room for at least three consecutive days. Animals were transferred into the testing room at least 1 hour before the start of testing. All behavioral tests were performed during the light phase of the circadian cycle between 09:00 and 17:00, and the room temperature was maintained at 22° ± 1°C. Sample sizes for each behavioral test were determined on the basis of the typical sample sizes used in the field. Animals are randomly assigned into treatment groups, with genotype and age balanced across groups. Behavioral data were analyzed by an experimenter blinded to both genotype and treatment condition. Data exclusion followed statistically criteria for outliers, defined as values exceeding three SDs from the mean. No data were excluded from the behavioral study.

#### Open-field test

Open-field exploration was assessed in a behavioral chamber with a dimension of 40 cm by 40 cm by 40 cm (RWD Life Science). Mice were placed in the open field for 10 min, and their movements were tracked with a video camera using the ANY maze software (Stoelting). The central zone was defined as the inner 9 squares (9/25 of total area), while the peripheral zone consisted of the 16 squares along the walls. Total distances traveled, center distances, and number of entries into the center were quantified

#### Y-maze novel arm exploration

During the training trial, one arm of the Y-maze (RWD Life Science) is blocked, allowing the animal to explore only two arms (the start arm and one other arm) for 10 min. The testing phase was conducted 1 hour after training, during which all three arms were accessible. Mice were allowed to explore all three arms for 5 min, and time spent in each arm and number of entries was quantified.

#### Y-maze spontaneous alternation

Mice were placed in the middle of a Y-maze and were allowed to freely explore all three arms for 5 min. Number of arm entries and number of alternations were determined. An arm entry was registered when all four limbs entered the arm. An alternation was registered when, during three consecutive arm visits, all three arms have been visited (e.g. 1-2-3, 3-1-2, 2-1-3, etc.). The alternation score was calculated by (number of alternations/number of visit triplets) × 100.

#### Three-chamber social interaction

The sociability of mice was determined using a three-chambered apparatus (60 cm by 40 cm by 22 cm; RWD Life Science). A test mouse was placed in the apparatus containing empty wire cages and was allowed to freely explore for 5 min for familiarization with the apparatus and baseline activity assessment. Subsequently, the mouse was restricted to the middle chamber, and a novel conspecific (M1, which has the same background, age, and gender as the test mouse) was randomly introduced into one of two identical cages located in the side chambers. The test mouse was allowed to explore freely for 10 min after opening the chamber doors, and its time spent in each of the three chambers and the time spent sniffing (within 2 cm of wire cages) were analyzed manually from video recordings. Social preference index was calculated as (time spent on M1 – time spent on empty cage)/(time spent on M1 + time spent on empty cage).

For a subset of the mice, a second test was performed on the following day to determine social recognition memory. Another mouse (M2) was introduced into one of the two side chamber cages in addition to M1. The test mouse was allowed to explore freely for 10 min, and its time spent in each of the three chambers and the time spent sniffing on M1 and M2 were analyzed manually. Social novelty index was calculated as (time spent on stranger M2 – time spent on familiar M1)/(time spent on stranger M2 + time spent on familiar M1).

#### Prepulse inhibition

The PPI test was adapted from a published protocol (87). The experimental apparatus (Shanghai Xinruan Information Technology Co. Ltd.) consists of a sound-attenuated chamber containing a restrainer mounted on a piezoelectric accelerometer for detecting startle responses. During the acclimation phase 1 day before testing, the test mouse was placed into an open-air cage and without any startle stimulus for 15 min. On the testing day, the session began with a 5-min habituation period, followed by two types of stimulus trials presented in a pseudorandom order: (i) pulse alone (a 120-dB, 40-ms stimulus) and (ii) prepulse pulse (a 120-dB, 40-ms stimulus preceded by a 71-, 76-, or 81-dB, 20-ms prepulse). Each trial was performed 10 times with a variable intertrial interval (15 to 20 s). In addition, a 65-dB background noise was introduced throughout the entire testing period to avoid the effects of ambient noise. PPIs for each prepulse-pulse trial were calculated as [(startle amplitude of pulse-alone trial-startle amplitude of prepulse-pulse trial)/startle response in the pulse-alone trial] × 100.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Electrophysiology data analysis

NMDAR currents were determined as current density, quantified by the area under the curve from the moment of drug application until 1 s after the drug application. Data analyses were conducted using the Clampfit 7.0 software and were graphed in GraphPad Prism 9.0. FEPSP slopes were defined as the maximum slope during 1 ms of the rising phase. The fEPSP slope for each 2-min time frame was obtained by averaging every four consecutive measurements. Analyses of fEPSPs were conducted using WinLTP.

#### Statistical analysis

For all in vitro electrophysiology recordings, the “n” value represents the number of cells. For in vivo electrophysiology and behavioral experiments, the n value represents the number of animals. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0. Direct comparisons made between two groups were analyzed using the two-tailed Student’s t test. Comparisons made between multiple groups were done using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc Šidák’s multiple-comparison test or a two-way ANOVA followed by post hoc Tukey’s multiple-comparison test. Dose-response curves are fitted using a three-parameter Hill equation. LogEC50 and top values are compared using an extra sum-of-squares F test. Statistical significance is defined as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001. Data are represented as mean ± SEM.

# Integrated Prediction System for Individualized Ovarian Stimulation and Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome Prevention: Algorithm Development and Validation

**Authors:** Jingjing Chen; Jianjuan Zhao; Huiyu Qiu; Yanhui Liu; Yunqi Zhang; Qicheng Sun; Yan Yi; Hongying Tang; Jing Zhao; Bin Xu; Qiong Zhang; Ge Yang; Hui Li; Junjie Liu; Zhongzhou Yang; Shaolin Liang; Yanping Li; Jing Fu; Javad Sarvestan; Fanghu Sun; Kuan-Hsun Lin

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Reproductive Medicine, Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, Changsha, Hunan, China | 2Clinical Research Center for Women’s Reproductive Health in Hunan Province, Changsha, China | 3Digital Health Lab, Institute for Six-sector Economy, Fudan University, Shanghai, China | 4Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, Changsha, China | 5Reproductive Medicine Department, The Third Affiliated Hospital of Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China | 6Division of Neonatology, Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangdong, China | 7School of Medicine, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangdong, China

## Abstract

Accurately predicting ovarian response and determining the optimal starting dose of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) remain critical yet challenging for effective ovarian stimulation. Currently, there is a lack of a comprehensive model capable of simultaneously forecasting the number of oocytes retrieved (NOR) and assessing the risk of early-onset moderate-to-severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

This study aimed to establish an integrated mode capable of forecasting the NOR and assessing the risk of early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS across varying starting doses of FSH.

This prognostic study included patients undergoing their first ovarian stimulation cycles at 2 independent in vitro fertilization clinics. Automated classifiers were used for variable selection. Machine learning models (11 for NOR and 11 for OHSS) were developed and validated using internal (n=6401) and external (n=3805) datasets. Shapley additive explanation was applied for variable interpretation. The best-performing models were incorporated into a web-based prediction tool.

For NOR prediction, 17 variables were selected, with the gradient boosting regressor achieving the highest performance (internal dataset: R2=0.7978; external dataset: R2=0.7924). For OHSS prediction, 19 variables were identified, and the LightGBM model demonstrated superior performance (internal dataset: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.7588; external dataset: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.7287). Shapley additive explanation analysis highlighted the FSH starting dose to BMI ratio and baseline antral follicle count as key predictors for NOR and OHSS, respectively. Dose-response curves were generated to visualize predicted outcomes with varying FSH starting doses. The models were implemented in a user-friendly, research-oriented online prototype, individualized ovarian stimulation guide (InOvaSGuide).

This study introduces an integrated framework for predicting NOR and early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS risk across different FSH doses. Future prospective evaluation is needed before clinical implementation.

Keywords: individualized ovarian stimulation, ovarian response, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, follicle-stimulating hormone, machine learning

## Introduction

Over the past decade, individualized ovarian stimulation has become a key strategy in in vitro fertilization (IVF). Determining an appropriate starting dose of exogenous follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is essential for balancing efficacy and safety. Although earlier clinical practice emphasized maximizing oocyte yield (the more, the better), current consensus favors achieving a moderate ovarian response to optimize live birth rates while minimizing patient discomfort and iatrogenic risks such as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). Therefore, accurate prediction of ovarian response before stimulation is critical for optimizing treatment outcomes [1-4].

Although biomarkers, including antral follicle count (AFC), anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) levels, and BMI, are well associated with ovarian response, substantial interindividual and intraindividual variability limits their predictive precision. Tailoring FSH doses based solely on these indicators has not consistently improved clinical outcomes [5,6], highlighting the need for more comprehensive, data-driven approaches that integrate a broader spectrum of clinical and biological factors.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer new opportunities for improving decision-making in assisted reproduction, with applications reported in semen analysis [7], blastocysts grading [8], and trigger-day assessments [9]. Several ML models have also been developed to predict the number of oocytes retrieved (NOR) [10-13] or to classify ovarian responsiveness [10]; however, most remain limited in scope. They typically rely on a narrow set of baseline features, adopt single-model frameworks, and focus predominantly on treatment efficacy such as oocyte yield, with relatively limited attention to safety outcomes, including OHSS. These limitations emphasize the need for predictive frameworks that simultaneously incorporate both efficacy and safety. Furthermore, despite multiple evidence-based algorithms for FSH dosing, considerable variability in ovarian response persists even among patients with comparable baseline characteristics. A model that jointly predicts NOR and OHSS risk across a range of FSH doses may provide useful predictive information and support dose-specific decision-making, helping clinicians consider the balance between efficacy and safety when selecting individualized FSH doses.

In this study, ML models were developed to predict NOR and early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS using datasets from 2 IVF centers. Models with optimal performance were integrated into a clinician-oriented decision support prototype, termed individualized ovarian stimulation guide (“InOvaSGuide”), complemented by a web-based calculator. For each patient, the system provides individualized dose-response curves that display predicted NOR and early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS probabilities across varying FSH starting doses, thus supporting personalized ovarian stimulation.

## Methods

### Ethical Considerations

This prognostic study was designed as a retrospective analysis and was approved by the Reproductive Medicine Ethics Committee of Xiangya Hospital (2021010) and the Medicine Ethics Committee of Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital (2024-LHQRMYY-KYLL-63). Informed consent was waived because all data were retrospectively collected from routine clinical records and anonymized before analysis. The study adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and followed the TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis; Table S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1) reporting guideline [14]. All data analyses were performed by an external team using anonymized data only, ensuring full protection of participant privacy. No compensation was provided to participants, as the study involved retrospective and fully anonymized data.

### Study Cohort

The inclusion criteria were (1) patients with the first ovarian stimulation cycle conducted between January 1, 2018, and September 30, 2022, at the Department of Reproductive Medicine of Xiangya Hospital (internal dataset) and between May 1, 2021, and December 30, 2023, at the Reproductive Center of Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital (external dataset) and (2) patients aged 20 to 40 years. Exclusion criteria were (1) patients with diminished ovarian reserve, diagnosed by AMH ≤1.1 ng/mL or baseline AFC ≤7 [15]; (2) patients using the microstimulation protocols for ovarian stimulation, including progestin-primed ovarian stimulation protocol, natural cycle protocol, etc; and (3) patients with more than 50% missingness in key clinical variables. Notably, patients with diminished ovarian reserve or those undergoing microstimulation protocols were excluded because these groups require highly individualized stimulation strategies, exhibit markedly lower oocyte yield, and have a substantially reduced risk of OHSS under comparable FSH exposure, which would have created pronounced class imbalance and reduced model robustness.

After screening, 6401 patients from Xiangya Hospital and 3805 from Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital were included in the internal and external datasets, respectively.

### Ovarian Stimulation Process and the Diagnosis of Early-Onset Moderate-to-Severe OHSS

Before commencing the IVF and intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycle, patients underwent a thorough physical examination, including the assessment of basic physical parameters (height, weight, and BMI), measurement of basal hormone levels (FSH, luteinizing hormone [LH], estradiol, testosterone, progesterone, prolactin, and AMH), biochemical tests (fasting glucose, fasting insulin, lipid levels, and thyroid hormones), and transvaginal ultrasonography for basal AFC. Subsequently, experienced physicians personalized the ovarian stimulation protocol and the starting dose of FSH based on comprehensive clinical assessment. Throughout stimulation, patients underwent monitoring via transvaginal ultrasonography and serum hormone assessments, with gonadotropin dosage adjustments made according to individual ovarian responses. Human chorionic gonadotropin or gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, alone or combined, triggered oocyte maturation when 3 or more follicles measuring 17 mm or greater were observed. Oocyte retrieval occurred 36 hours after triggering, and the NOR was recorded. Eligible patients underwent fresh embryo transfer with 1 or 2 embryos.

The study primarily focused on the occurrence of early-onset, moderate-to-severe OHSS, which was diagnosed within 9 days after triggering based on established guidelines [16], considering both clinical and laboratory features. All relevant individual and clinical variables during the process were obtained from the clinical database for feature screening and selection.

### Data Preprocessing and Feature Selection

All data analysis was performed by an external team using anonymized data, ensuring full protection of participant privacy. To elucidate correlations between predictive features and clinical outcomes with an emphasis on medical interpretability, we performed feature engineering on selected variables. This process resulted in 2 additional variables: “FSH to LH ratio” and “FSH starting dose to BMI ratio,” which improved predictive accuracy while maintaining transparency and clinical relevance. Furthermore, to address skewness and improve distributional normality, a logarithmic transformation was applied to AMH, triglycerides, and FSH/LH (Figures S1 and S2 in Multimedia Appendix 1). Missing data were handled using mean imputation, with feature-wise means computed exclusively from the training set and subsequently applied to the test and external validation sets, to prevent information leakage. The overall proportion of missingness was low, and imputation did not materially alter variable distributions.

To identify key variables, we applied feature importance–based selection using the Boruta algorithm, performed exclusively within the training dataset (Figures S3 and S4 in Multimedia Appendix 1). This approach led to the selection of 17 variables for the NOR prediction model and 19 variables for the OHSS prediction model.

### NOR Model Development

In the prediction of NOR, 17 features, including starting dose of FSH to BMI ratio, BMI, log (AMH), and specifically the ovarian stimulation protocol, were selected. The NOR divided by the starting dose of FSH was used and logarithmically transformed as the outcome variable with improved predictive performance. For model training, the internal dataset was divided into an 8:2 split, with 79.9% (5120/6401) of the data randomly allocated to the training set and the remaining 20% (1281/6401) assigned to the internal test set. All data from the external dataset were held out entirely and used exclusively as an external validation cohort, providing an independent assessment of model generalizability across institutions. Eleven ML algorithms, including a linear regression model, were trained to predict the preprocessed NOR outcome. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using 5-fold cross-validation within the training set only, with all hyperparameters predefined and summarized in Table S2 in Multimedia Appendix 1. Model performance was assessed using 4 key metrics: R2, adjusted R2, mean absolute error, and root mean square error.

### OHSS Model Development

For OHSS prediction, the target variable was the occurrence of early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS. Given the low event rate and resulting class imbalance, several commonly used imbalances handling strategies (eg, oversampling, undersampling, and ensemble-based resampling) were evaluated. Cost-sensitive learning was ultimately adopted, assigning differentiated penalties to misclassifications while preserving all original clinical data distribution. To prevent overfitting, model complexity was controlled by limiting the number of parameters and applying regularization techniques, as appropriate for each algorithm. Eleven ML algorithms were implemented, with corresponding hyperparameters detailed in Table S3 in Multimedia Appendix 1. As with the NOR model, hyperparameter optimization was conducted exclusively within the training set, and model performance was evaluated on both the internal and the external datasets using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), the precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC), recall, specificity, weighted F1-score, Cohen κ, and positive and negative predictive values.

### Shapley Additive Explanation Value

To further explore the significant features driving the model’s predictions, we used the Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) analysis to assess the importance of core features. SHAP serves as an interpretative tool for ensemble tree models, offering a detailed breakdown of the influence of input features on predictions.

### Creation of Dose-Response Curves

In this study, 2 distinct models were developed: a classification model for predicting early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS and a regression model for forecasting NOR. Models of best performance were incorporated into an integrated, research-oriented computational system, complemented by a web-based calculator. By inputting baseline patient characteristics, the system generates predictions for NOR and early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS probability, presented as a dose-response curve illustrating changes with increasing FSH starting doses.

### Statistical Analysis

The baseline characteristics of patients between the internal dataset and the external dataset were compared using the chi-square test for categorical variables. For continuous variables, we assessed normality using the Shapiro-Wilk W test. Depending on the results, we used either the 2-tailed Student t test or the Mann-Whitney U test for comparison. R Studio (version 4.3.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing), Python (version 3.11.4; Python Software Foundation), the open-source scikit-learn package (version 3.9.13; open-source community-developed Python ML library), LightGBM (version 4.3.0; Microsoft Corporation), and XGBoost (version 2.0.0; open-source project maintained by XGBoost contributors) were used for model development and statistical analyses.

## Results

### The Integrated Ovarian Response Prediction System

To address the challenges of individualized ovarian stimulation, we developed an integrated prediction system, “InOvaSGuide,” designed to predict both the NOR and the probability of early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS before ovarian stimulation. The system was built using datasets from 2 IVF clinics and incorporates 2 distinct ML models for NOR and OHSS predictions, respectively (Figure 1A). By analyzing patients’ baseline characteristics, the system generates dose-response curves that illustrate the predicted benefit (NOR) and risk (early-onset moderate-to-severe OHSS) across varying FSH starting doses (Figures 1B and C). Additionally, a user-friendly web-based calculator was developed to enhance accessibility and support exploratory use in clinically relevant contexts (Figure S7 in Multimedia Appendix 1).
