# Explicit Almost-Optimal $\varepsilon$ -Balanced Codes via Free Expander Walks

**Authors:** Jun-Ting Hsieh ††thanks: MIT. juntingh@mit.edu. Sidhanth Mohanty ††thanks: Northwestern University. sidhanth.mohanty@northwestern.edu. Rachel Yun Zhang ††thanks: MIT. rachelyz@mit.edu. Supported by the Schwarzman College of Computing Future Research Fellowship supported by Google.

## Abstract

We study the problem of constructing explicit binary codes whose rate and distance match the Gilbert–Varshamov bound in the low-rate, high-distance regime. In 2017, Ta-Shma [27] gave an explicit family of codes where every pair of codewords has relative distance $\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2}$ , with rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^{2+o(1)})$ , matching the Gilbert–Varshamov bound up to a factor of $\varepsilon^{o(1)}$ . Ta-Shma’s construction was based on starting with a good code and amplifying its bias with walks arising from the $s$ -wide-replacement product.

In this work, we give a simpler almost-optimal construction, based on what we call free expander walks—ordinary expander walks where each step is taken on a distinct expander from a carefully chosen sequence. This sequence of expanders is derived from the construction of near- $X$ -Ramanujan graphs due to O’Donnell and Wu [26]. We additionally discuss some additional applications of near- $X$ -Ramanujan graphs to “on average” lossless expansion and rotating expanders.

## 1 Introduction

A longstanding and fundamental open problem in coding theory is to construct binary codes with the best possible tradeoffs between rate and distance. In this work, we seek to understand the best possible rate achievable by a code family whose relative distance approaches $\frac{1}{2}$ . The classical Gilbert–Varshamov (GV) bound guarantees the existence of a binary code family with relative distance $\geqslant\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon$ and rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^{2})$ — indeed, a random linear code satisfies such a property; this is tight up to a $\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ factor due to the lower bound of [23] (see also [4]). However, constructing explicit codes meeting this rate-distance tradeoff is not yet known and represents an important open problem.

Following [27], we seek to construct what are known as $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes, where the relative distance between any pair of codewords is in the interval $\left[\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2},\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}\right]$ . Notice that the property of being $\varepsilon$ -balanced is more restrictive than having relative distance $\geqslant\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon$ , which simply requires that the relative distance between every pair of codewords is bounded below by $\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon$ .

In the context of error-correction, explicit constructions of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes often have structure that plays well with designing fast decoding algorithms [1, 19, 20], a feature that random linear codes do not enjoy. In pseudorandomness, constructions of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes immediately give constructions of almost $k$ -wise uniform distribution [25], which is an important primitive in a myriad of applications: derandomization [25], probabilistically checkable proofs [5], constructing PRGs for restricted classes of functions [10], expander constructions [24, 26], and constructing explicit quantum codes [17] to name a few.

Obtaining explicit constructions of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes achieving the GV bound is an active thread in coding and pseudorandomness. One popular approach for constructing good codes is to concatenate a large alphabet code with a small binary code [21]. In the $\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon$ relative distance regime, explicit codes obtained via concatenation achieve rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^{3})$ , a result traditionally attributed to Zyablov [28]; see [11, Exercise 10.3] for an English presentation. A second approach for obtaining good $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes, pioneered by Rozenman and Wigderson and exposited in the lecture notes of Bogdanov [6], is to amplify bias via expander walks. In the original presentation, such expander walk-based codes obtained only a rate of $\Omega(\varepsilon^{4})$ . In 2017, the breakthrough work of Ta-Shma [27] showed how to sparsify these expander walks using a wide replacement product, thereby obtaining an explicit family of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes with rate $\Omega\left(\varepsilon^{2+o(1)}\right)$ , matching the GV bound up to a subpolynomial factor in $1/\varepsilon$ . The subpolynomial factor was recently improved in [7].

In this work, we present what we believe is a much simpler explicit construction of a nearly optimal $\varepsilon$ -balanced code with rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^{2+o(1)})$ .

#### Theorem 1.1.

There is an explicit $\varepsilon$ -balanced binary linear code $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}$ with rate $\Omega\left\lparen\varepsilon^{2+o(1)}\right\rparen$ .

Our code family is obtained by taking the simple expander walk, with a different expander at each step. While we obtain a worse subpolynomial error term than that achieved by [27, 7], we hope that our simplification can lead to progress in both explicit constructions and algorithms.

#### Remark 1.2.

The work of Jeronimo, Mittal, Roy, and Wigderson [18] proved that Ta-Shma’s construction extends to amplifying bias in the operator setting as well, a fact useful in constructing almost-optimal expanders on groups. In contrast, it is possible to construct operators for which our construction fails to achieve almost-optimal amplification.

### 1.1 Overview

To motivate our construction, we begin by discussing a construction based on expander walks that achieves rate $\Omega(\varepsilon^{4})$ , which is also the starting point for Ta-Shma’s construction.

Given a code $\mathcal{C}_{0}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{0}}$ with bias $\varepsilon_{0}$ , rate $r_{0}$ , and block length $n_{0}$ , we may consider the code $\mathcal{C}$ obtained as an expander walk lift with block length $n_{0}\cdot d^{\ell}$ obtained by taking a $d$ -regular $\lambda$ -spectral expander $G$ , and defining the codewords to be $f(x)_{i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}}\coloneqq x_{i_{0}}+\dots+x_{i_{\ell}}$ where $x\in\mathcal{C}_{0}$ and $i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell}$ is a length- $\ell$ walk in $G$ .

The bias can be written as $\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}(A_{G}D_{x})^{\ell}\mathbf{1}\right\rangle$ , where $A_{G}$ is the normalized adjacency matrix of $G$ , $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-1s vector, $D_{x}$ is an $n_{0}\times n_{0}$ diagonal matrix where the $(i,i)$ -th entry is $(-1)^{x_{i}}$ , and $\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle$ is the normalized inner product. One may use spectral properties of $A_{G}$ to prove that $\left\lVert(A_{G}D_{x})^{2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\lambda$ , which in turn implies that the bias is at most $\lambda^{\ell/2}$ . Since we can choose $\lambda$ to be $\Theta\left\lparen\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\right\rparen$ , one obtains a rate of $\Omega(\varepsilon^{4})$ .

Another way to visualize the effect of the walk $(A_{G}D_{x})^{\ell}$ is via the following schematic, in which arrows represent how mass may move along the $\mathbf{1}$ and $\perp$ directions (orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$ ) by applications of $D_{x}$ and $A_{G}$ . The unlabeled black arrows represent an upper bound of $1$ , i.e., it’s possible that an application of $D_{x}$ or $A_{G}$ does not shrink the norm of the vector. The norm of the vector obtained by successive applications of $A_{G}D_{x}$ can be thought of as the maximum over all paths through the diagram of the product of all of the factors it passes through.

Consider the following highlighted path that switches between the $\mathbf{1}$ and $\perp$ components on every application of $D_{x}$ . This path only picks up a $\lambda$ factor in every other application of $A_{G}$ , explaining why we may only experience a $\lambda^{\ell/2}$ decay over $\ell$ steps.

It is natural to wonder whether the bound of $\lambda$ for two steps of the walk can be improved to a $\lambda^{2}$ . Indeed, such an improvement would immediately imply Theorem 1.1. Unfortunately, it is possible to instantiate a graph $G$ along with $x$ such that the bias is genuinely as large as $\lambda^{\ell/2}$ . Consider for instance $x$ that is the second eigenvector of $A_{G}$ : the highlighted path precisely describes the evolution of successive applications of $A_{G}D_{x}$ .

Free expander walks. In general, the $\lambda^{\ell/2}$ decay is realized if $x$ aligns with an atypically sparse or abnormally dense cut in $G$ . Our way around this is to take each step on a different expander. If we have an ensemble of expanders $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ that “look pseudorandom” to each other, then no fixed $x$ can align with an abnormal cut in many of the $H_{i}$ , and in fact $x$ should “look random” to most of them. Concretely, we assume an ensemble of $\lambda$ -spectral expanders $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ satisfying the all-signings near-Ramanujan property, i.e.

$$ \max_{\sigma:[t]\to\{\pm 1\}}\max_{y:\left\langle y,\mathbf{1}\right\rangle=0}\mathbf{E}_{\bm{i}\sim[t]}\frac{\left\langle y,\sigma_{\bm{i}}A_{H_{\bm{i}}}y\right\rangle}{\left\langle y,y\right\rangle}\leqslant\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{t}}\,. $$

Explicit constructions of such ensembles are implied by the work of O’Donnell and Wu [26].

Given such an ensemble of expanders, it is not too hard to show that for most graphs $H_{i}$ , most of the mass in the $\mathbf{1}$ direction cannot return to the $\mathbf{1}$ direction after just one step according to $H_{i}$ . More generally, we show that even for larger numbers of steps, most sequences $H_{i_{1}},\dots,H_{i_{\kappa}}$ will not cause most of the mass to return to the $\mathbf{1}$ direction. Precisely, we show that for any given $x$ , a random word $\bm{w}$ in $[t]^{\kappa}$ of not-too-large length $\kappa$ satisfies $\left\lVert A_{H_{\bm{w}_{\kappa}}}D_{x}\cdots A_{H_{\bm{w}_{1}}}D_{x}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\lambda^{\kappa-1}$ with high probability. Thus, if we perform an expander walk whose schedule includes every word in $[t]^{\kappa}$ , then we obtain an almost-optimal spectral norm bound on most words.

### 1.2 Organization

In Section 2, we present the construction based on ensembles satisfying the all-signings near-Ramanujan property, along with the proof of Theorem 1.1.

In Section 3, we give a brief description of the construction of “free expanders” by O’Donnell and Wu [26] and how the ensembles we use arise as a special case. We also show a few other properties of these ensembles and some applications of their result, including “on-average” lossless expansion and rotating expanders. These applications are of independent interest, and we hope that they draw further attention to these objects.

## 2 Almost-Optimal $\varepsilon$ -Balanced Codes

### 2.1 Ingredients and Notation

In this paper, we find it more convenient to present our definitions and proofs for binary codes in the $\{\pm 1\}$ -basis, instead of the $\{0,1\}$ -basis. In this $\{\pm 1\}$ -basis, binary linear codes correspond to multiplicative subspaces of $\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ . One can convert from the $\{0,1\}$ -basis (and back) via the map $x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\longleftrightarrow((-1)^{x_{i}})_{i\in[n]}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ .

#### Definition 2.1 (Binary codes).

A binary code is a subset $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ . It is said to be linear if it is in fact a multiplicative subspace of $\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ . Its dimension is $\log_{2}|\mathcal{C}|$ , and its rate is $\frac{\log_{2}|\mathcal{C}|}{n}$ .

We will be interested in binary linear codes with relative distance between $\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2}$ and $\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}$ . In the multiplicative notation, this corresponds to the code having bias $\leqslant\varepsilon$ .

#### Definition 2.2 (Bias).

We will say that a string $x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ has bias $\varepsilon$ if $\mathsf{bias}(x)\coloneqq|\mathbb{E}_{i\in[n]}x_{i}|=\varepsilon$ . We say that a binary linear code $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n}$ has bias $\leqslant\varepsilon$ if for all $x\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{1^{n}\}$ , $\mathsf{bias}(x)\leqslant\varepsilon$ .

Base code. Let $\mathcal{C}_{0}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}}$ be an explicit linear code of block length $n_{0}$ , bias $\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}\in(0,1/4]$ , and rate $r_{0}=\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon_{0})>0$ . For concreteness, we can take $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ to be the construction of [3]. We will later choose $\varepsilon_{0}$ to depend on our target bias $\varepsilon$ .

Graphs, matrices, and inner product. For a graph $G$ , we use $A_{G}$ to denote its normalized adjacency matrix. We use $\mathbf{1}$ to refer to the all-ones vector. For $x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}}$ we set $D_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(x)$ . Throughout, we use the normalized inner product, for functions $f,g:[n_{0}]\to\mathbb{R}$ , we define $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle\coloneqq\mathbf{E}_{\bm{v}\sim[n_{0}]}f(\bm{v})\cdot g(\bm{v})$ , and write $\left\lVert f\right\rVert\coloneqq\sqrt{\left\langle f,f\right\rangle}$ for the induced norm.

All-signings near-Ramanujan families. We now describe the kind of expander family we use for defining our expander walk.

#### Definition 2.3.

We say that a collection of $d$ -regular graphs $(H_{j})_{j\in[t]}$ on the same vertex set $V$ is an all-signings near-Ramanujan family if for every signing $\sigma\in\{\pm 1\}^{t}$ , the signed $td$ -regular multigraph

$$ H(\sigma)\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sigma_{j}H_{j} $$

satisfies $\left\lVert A_{H(\sigma)}|_{\mathbf{1}^{\perp}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{td}}$ , and further, $\left\lVert A_{H_{j}}|_{\mathbf{1}^{\perp}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ for all $j\in[t]$ .

Note that a Ramanujan $d$ -regular graph $H$ has $\left\lVert A_{H}|_{\mathbf{1}^{\perp}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\frac{2\sqrt{d-1}}{d}$ , which is smaller than $\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ . In Definition 2.3, We use the bounds $\frac{2}{\sqrt{td}}$ and $\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ because we only have constructions of near-Ramanujan families (and also for simplicity).

#### Theorem 2.4 (Special case of [26, Theorem 10.13]).

For every $t\geqslant 1$ , and $d\geqslant 2$ , there is an explicit all-signings near-Ramanujan family $\{G_{n_{0}}\}_{n_{0}\in\mathbb{N}}$ where $G_{n_{0}}$ is on a vertex set $V_{n_{0}}$ such that $|V_{n_{0}}|=n_{0}+o(n_{0})$ .

#### Remark 2.5.

For a reader interested in understanding the proof of Theorem 2.4, the simplest self-contained route is to check that the construction of Mohanty, O’Donnell, and Paredes [24] can be adapted to satisfy this property. Here we simply appeal to the far-reaching generalization of [24] given by O’Donnell and Wu [26, Theorem 10.13].

#### Remark 2.6.

For a fixed signing, the signed sum of a collection of independent random graphs is near-Ramanujan with high probability. Since there are only constantly many signings, by the union bound, a random ensemble is all-signings near-Ramanujan. The construction of [26] is obtained by derandomizing the randomized construction, and hence it is natural that it inherits this basic property.

### 2.2 The Construction

Fix integers $t\geqslant 2$ and $d$ . Using Theorem 2.4, we construct an all-signings near-Ramanujan family of $d$ -regular graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ on $[n_{0}]$ .11 1 Strictly speaking, for a given $n_{0}$ , we have $|V(H_{1},\dots,H_{t})|=n_{0}+o(n_{0})$ . However, we can pad the base code with zeros if necessary, so the block length is equal to the number of vertices and incur only a $1+o(1)$ blowup in block length. The following definition formally articulates the notion of a free expander walk.

#### Definition 2.7 (Expander walk lift).

Given a word $W\in[t]^{\ell}$ and $x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}}$ , we define its $W$ -expander walk lift $f_{W}(x)\in\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}\cdot d^{\ell}}$ as follows. Let $I_{W}$ denote the set of all length- $\ell$ walks $(i_{0},i_{1},\dots,i_{\ell})\in[n_{0}]^{\ell+1}$ , where $i_{0}\in[n_{0}]$ and $i_{s}$ is a neighbor of $i_{s-1}$ in $H_{W[s]}$ for all $s\in[\ell]$ . The coordinates of $f_{W}(x)$ are indexed by walks $i=(i_{0},i_{1},\dots,i_{\ell})\in I_{W}$ , and we set

$$ f_{W}(x)_{i}=x_{i_{0}}\cdot x_{i_{1}}\cdots x_{i_{\ell}}\,. $$

For example, a word $W=(1,2,3)$ gives rise to $n_{0}d^{3}$ length-3 walks ( $i_{0},i_{1},i_{2},i_{3})$ , where $(i_{0},i_{1})\in E(H_{1})$ , $(i_{1},i_{2})\in E(H_{2})$ , and $(i_{2},i_{3})\in E(H_{3})$ .

We now describe the word $W$ that gives the sequence of expanders we use in our construction.

#### Definition 2.8 (Expander schedule).

For some integers $\kappa$ and $r$ , let $\ell\coloneqq\kappa\cdot t^{\kappa}\cdot r$ and construct $W^{*}\in[t]^{\ell}$ by concatenating all words in $[t]^{\kappa}$ in an arbitrary order, and then repeating this $r$ times; i.e.,

$$ W^{*}=\underbrace{w^{(1)}_{1}\,\cdots\,w^{(1)}_{\kappa}}_{w^{(1)}\in[t]^{\kappa}}\;\;\Big\|\;\;\underbrace{w^{(2)}_{1}\,\cdots\,w^{(2)}_{\kappa}}_{w^{(2)}\in[t]^{\kappa}}\;\;\Big\|\;\;\cdots\;\;\Big\|\;\;\underbrace{w^{(r\cdot t^{\kappa})}_{1}\,\cdots\,w^{(r\cdot t^{\kappa})}_{\kappa}}_{w^{(r\cdot t^{\kappa})}\in[t]^{\kappa}}\,, $$

so $W^{*}$ has length $\ell$ .

Construction of our code and parameter settings. Henceforth, we define $f\coloneqq f_{W^{*}}$ , and define our code $\mathcal{C}$ as the image $f(\mathcal{C}_{0})\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}d^{\ell}}$ . Linearity of $\mathcal{C}$ follows from multiplicativity of $f$ .

We will set $t=d^{2}$ , and define $\lambda\coloneqq\max\left\{\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}},\varepsilon_{0}\right\}$ , where $\varepsilon_{0}$ is the bias of the base code $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ .

#### Remark 2.9.

We remind the reader that we are working with codes in the $\{\pm 1\}$ basis rather than the standard $\{0,1\}$ basis. In the $\{0,1\}$ basis, the expander walk lift code would have codewords $\widehat{f}(\widehat{x})_{(i_{0},\dots,i_{\ell})}=\widehat{x}_{i_{0}}\oplus\widehat{x}_{i_{1}}\oplus\cdots\oplus\widehat{x}_{i_{\ell}}$ for $\widehat{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n_{0}}$ .

### 2.3 Analyzing the Construction

Consider $x\in\mathcal{C}_{0}\backslash\{\mathbf{1}\}$ . We can write:

$$ \mathsf{bias}(f(x))=\left|\big\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{H_{\ell}}D_{x}A_{H_{\ell-1}}\cdots D_{x}A_{H_{1}}D_{x}\mathbf{1}\big\rangle\right|, $$

where $D_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(x)$ and $A_{H_{s}}=\frac{1}{d}\mathrm{Adj}(H_{s})$ where $\mathrm{Adj}(H_{s})\in\{0,1\}^{n_{0}\times n_{0}}$ denotes the adjacency matrix of $H_{s}$ . Indeed, starting from the uniform distribution on $[n_{0}]$ , each application of $D_{x}$ multiplies the current coordinate by $x_{i}$ , and each $A_{H_{s}}$ takes a uniform step to a neighbor in $H_{s}$ .

We now introduce some notation to streamline the subsequent proofs.

- • We use $\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}$ to denote the projection onto the $\mathbf{1}$ direction, and $\Pi_{\perp}$ for the projection onto the subspace orthogonal to $\mathbf{1}$ .

- • We use $A_{j}$ as shorthand for $A_{H_{j}}$ .

- • Given a sequence of matrices $Q_{1},\dots,Q_{k}$ , we will use $\prod_{i=1}^{k}Q_{i}$ to denote $Q_{k}\cdots Q_{1}$ .

- • Given a word $w\in[t]^{\kappa}$ , we define $M_{w}\coloneqq A_{w_{\kappa}}D_{x}\cdots A_{w_{1}}D_{x}$ .

With this notation in hand, we may write

$$ \mathsf{bias}(f(x))=\left\lvert\big\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}M_{w^{(r\cdot t^{\kappa})}}\cdots M_{w^{(1)}}\mathbf{1}\big\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\prod_{j=1}^{r\cdot t^{\kappa}}\left\lVert M_{w^{(j)}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\,. $$

The key technical lemma is the following.

#### Lemma 2.10.

Let $\bm{w}$ be a uniformly random word drawn from $[t]^{\kappa}$ , where $t=d^{2}$ . Then, for any $x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n_{0}}$ with $\mathsf{bias}(x)\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}$ , with probability at least $1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}$ , we have $\left\lVert M_{\bm{w}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 2^{\kappa+1}\lambda^{\kappa-1}$ . Recall that $M_{w}$ implicitly depends on $x$ .

For the remaining $\leqslant\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}$ fraction of the $w\in[t]^{\kappa}$ not satisfying the above bound on $\lVert M_{w}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ , we use the following trivial bound.

#### Observation 2.11.

For every $w\in[t]^{\kappa}$ , we have $\left\lVert M_{w}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 1$ .

#### Proof.

This is immediate from combining sub-multiplicativity of the operator norm with the fact that $M_{w}$ is a product of matrices with operator norm at most $1$ . ∎

As an immediate corollary of Lemma 2.10 and Observation 2.11, we obtain the following.

#### Lemma 2.12.

Let $x\in\mathcal{C}_{0}\setminus\{\mathbf{1}\}$ of bias $\varepsilon_{0}$ . The bias of $f(x)$ is at most

$$ \lambda^{\ell\cdot\left\lparen 1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{\kappa}\right\rparen}\cdot 2^{\ell\cdot\frac{\kappa+1}{\kappa}}\,. $$

With Lemma 2.12 in hand, we are ready to prove Theorem 1.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Consider the concrete parameter setting in terms of some $\varepsilon^{\prime}>0$ :

$$ \displaystyle d=\left\lceil\exp\left\lparen\sqrt{\log\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}\right\rparen\right\rceil\,,\quad t=d^{2}\,,\quad\kappa=\left\lfloor\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{\log\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}\right\rfloor\,,\quad r=\left\lceil{\frac{2\log_{d}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}{\kappa t^{\kappa}}}\right\rceil\,,\quad\varepsilon_{0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\,,\quad $$

so that $\lambda=\max\{\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}},\varepsilon_{0}\}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ . For simplicity, we will use $o(1)$ to denote any term at most $\frac{O(1)}{\sqrt{\log\log(1/\varepsilon^{\prime})}}$ . With this notation, $\frac{1}{\log d}$ and $\frac{1}{\kappa}$ are both $o(1)$ .

We first verify that $r\geqslant 1/o(1)$ . Note that $\kappa t^{\kappa}\log d=\kappa e^{2\kappa\log d}\log d\leqslant(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\prime}})^{1/4}\cdot O(\log\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{\prime}})$ . Thus, we have that $r=\left\lceil\frac{2\log(1/\varepsilon^{\prime})}{\kappa t^{\kappa}\log d}\right\rceil\geqslant 1/o(1)$ . Next, observe that $r$ is set such that $\ell=\kappa t^{\kappa}r=2\log_{d}(1/\varepsilon^{\prime})\cdot(1+o(1))$ (the error term is because of the ceiling), thus $d^{-\frac{1}{2}\ell}=(\varepsilon^{\prime})^{1-o(1)}$ .

From Lemma 2.12, we have that for all $x\in\mathcal{C}_{0}\setminus\{\mathbf{1}\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{bias}(f(x)) \displaystyle\leqslant\lambda^{\ell\cdot\left\lparen 1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{\kappa}\right\rparen}\cdot 2^{\ell\cdot\frac{\kappa+1}{\kappa}}\leqslant 2^{2\ell}\cdot d^{-\frac{1}{2}\ell\left\lparen 1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{\kappa}\right\rparen}\,. $$

Both $\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}$ and $\frac{1}{\kappa}\leqslant o(1)$ , and $2^{2\ell}=(1/\varepsilon^{\prime})^{O(1/\log d)}=(\varepsilon^{\prime})^{-o(1)}$ . Thus, the bias of our code is $(\varepsilon^{\prime})^{1-o(1)}$ .

On the other hand, the rate of the code is $\Omega(\varepsilon_{0}^{4})\cdot d^{-\ell}$ , where $\Omega(\varepsilon_{0}^{4})$ is the rate of the base code $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ , and $d^{\ell}$ is the total number of length- $\ell$ walks. Then, $\varepsilon_{0}^{4}d^{-\ell}=d^{-\ell(1+\frac{2}{\ell})}=(\varepsilon^{\prime})^{2+o(1)}$ .

The theorem statement follows by choosing $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon^{1+o(1)}$ for a suitably chosen $o(1)$ term. The $o(1)$ in the statement of Theorem 1.1 is precisely $\frac{O(1)}{\sqrt{\log\log(1/\varepsilon)}}$ . ∎

### 2.4 Proof of Lemma 2.10

It now remains to prove Lemma 2.10. In service of doing so, we introduce the notion of a contractive sequence.

#### Definition 2.13 (Contractive sequence).

We say that $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{\kappa})\in[t]^{\kappa}$ is a contractive sequence if for every $1\leqslant r<s\leqslant\kappa$ , we have:

$$ \left\lvert\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}\Pi_{\perp}A_{w_{s-1}}D_{x}\Pi_{\perp}A_{w_{s-2}}\dots D_{x}\Pi_{\perp}A_{w_{r}}D_{x}\mathbf{1}\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\lambda^{s-r+1}. $$

We remark that there are $s-r$ copies of $A_{w_{i}}$ in the above equation, and thus the naive bound from second eigenvalue considerations alone is a bound of $\leqslant\lambda^{s-r}$ . Contractive sequences shrink more than the naive bound by a factor of $\lambda$ .

#### Observation 2.14.

Every nonempty subsequence of a contractive sequence $w$ is contractive.

Lemma 2.10 then readily follows from Lemmas 2.15 and 2.16 below.

#### Lemma 2.15.

Let $\bm{w}\sim[t]^{\kappa}$ be drawn uniformly at random. For $t=d^{2}$ , with probability $1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}$ , $\bm{w}$ is a contractive sequence.

#### Lemma 2.16.

Let $w$ be a contractive sequence. Then it holds that $\lVert M_{w}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 2^{\kappa+1}\lambda^{\kappa-1}$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 2.15: Most sequences are contractive

#### Proof of Lemma 2.15.

Note that for any $w\in[t]$ , $A_{w}$ commutes with $\Pi_{\perp}$ , and hence the claim is equivalent to proving:

$$ \left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{w_{s-1}}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}A_{w_{s-2}}\Pi_{\perp}\cdots D_{x}A_{w_{r}}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\lambda^{s-r+1}\,. $$

We will first prove that for any $y$ such that $\left\langle y,\mathbf{1}\right\rangle=0$ , we have $\mathbf{E}_{\bm{u}\sim[t]}\left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{td}}\left\lVert y\right\rVert$ . We may prove this by expanding:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{E}_{\bm{u}\sim[t]}\left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle\right\rvert \displaystyle=\mathbf{E}_{\bm{u}\sim[t]}\mathrm{sign}\left\lparen\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle\right\rparen\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle D_{x}\mathbf{1},\ \mathbf{E}_{\bm{u}\sim[t]}\left[\mathrm{sign}\left\lparen\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle\right\rparen A_{\bm{u}}\right]\cdot y\right\rangle \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{td}}\left\lVert y\right\rVert\,, $$

where the last inequality uses the all-signings near-Ramanujan property. By Markov’s inequality, with probability at least $1-t^{-1/4}$ , for $\bm{u}\sim[t]$ we have:

$$ \left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{u}}y\right\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{2}{t^{1/4}\sqrt{d}}\left\lVert y\right\rVert\leqslant\lambda^{2}\left\lVert y\right\rVert\,. $$

where the last inequality used the concrete choice of $\lambda$ and $t=d^{2}$ .

Using the fact that $\left\lVert A_{H_{w_{i}}}|_{\mathbf{1}^{\perp}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}\leqslant\lambda$ , with probability at least $1-\frac{1}{t^{1/4}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}A_{\bm{w}_{s-1}}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}A_{\bm{w}_{s-2}}\Pi_{\perp}\cdots D_{x}A_{\bm{w}_{r}}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\lambda^{2}\left\lVert D_{x}A_{w_{s-2}}\Pi_{\perp}\cdots A_{w_{r}}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}\mathbf{1}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leqslant\lambda^{2}\cdot\lambda^{s-r-1} \displaystyle\leqslant\lambda^{s-r+1}\,. $$

Taking a union bound over all choices of $r$ and $s$ implies that $\bm{w}$ is a contractive sequence with probability at least $1-\frac{\kappa^{2}}{t^{1/4}}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 2.16: Bounds for operator norm of contractive sequences

The proof proceeds by separately analyzing the effect of $M_{w}$ on $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^{\perp}$ .

#### Lemma 2.17.

For any nonnegative integer $\kappa$ , and any contractive sequence $w\in[t]^{\kappa}$ , it holds that

$$ \lVert M_{w}\mathbf{1}\rVert\leqslant(2\lambda)^{\kappa}\,. $$

#### Proof.

We will prove this lemma by induction on $\kappa$ . For $\kappa=0$ , the statement is clear: $\lVert\mathbf{1}\rVert=1=(2\lambda)^{0}$ . Next, for $\kappa\geqslant 1$ , by iteratively splitting by projection onto $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^{\perp}$ after each step, we obtain the following decomposition:

$$ \displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}= \displaystyle~\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}+\sum_{s=1}^{\kappa}~\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\Bigg(\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}A_{s}D_{x}\Bigg)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\,. $$

Thus, by triangle inequality, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\leqslant \displaystyle~\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert \displaystyle+\sum_{s=1}^{\kappa}~\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\Bigg(\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}A_{s}D_{x}\Bigg)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\,. $$

Let us analyze each component of the right hand side of this expression.

- • First we analyze $\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert$ . For any vector $u$ and for any $j\in[\kappa]$ , we have that $\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}u$ is a vector perpendicular to $\mathbf{1}$ and one can bound its norm as follows:

$$ \lVert\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}u\rVert=\lVert A_{j}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}u\rVert\leqslant\lambda\lVert\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}u\rVert\leqslant\lambda\lVert D_{x}u\rVert\leqslant\lambda\lVert u\rVert\,, $$

where the first equality holds because $\Pi_{\perp}$ and $A_{j}$ commute since $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of $A_{j}$ . Thus, inductively applying $\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}$ to $\mathbf{1}$ , we have that

$$ \left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\leqslant\lambda^{\kappa}\,. $$

- • Next, let us consider $\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\Big(\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}A_{s}D_{x}\Big)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert$ for each $s\in[\kappa]$ . Since $\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}A_{s}=\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}$ , this is also equal to $\displaystyle\Bigg\|\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)$ $\displaystyle\Bigg(\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}D_{x}\Bigg)\left(\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\Bigg\|$ $\displaystyle=\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\cdot\left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{s-1}\Pi_{\perp}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right\rvert$ $\displaystyle\leqslant\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=s+1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\cdot\lambda^{s}$ $\displaystyle\leqslant(2\lambda)^{\kappa-s}\cdot\lambda^{s}\,.$ In the above, the penultimate inequality follows from the fact that $w_{1},\dots,w_{s-1}$ is a contractive sequence for $s\geqslant 2$ , and by the fact that for $s=1$ , $\left\lvert\left\langle\mathbf{1},D_{x}\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}\leqslant\lambda$ . The final inequality is from strong induction on the subsequence $w_{s+1},\dots,w_{\kappa}$ also being a contractive sequence.

Now, returning to Equation 3, we get that

$$ \left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)\mathbf{1}\right\rVert\leqslant\lambda^{\kappa}+\sum_{s=1}^{\kappa}2^{\kappa-s}\lambda^{\kappa}=(2\lambda)^{\kappa}\,.\qed $$

#### Lemma 2.18.

For any contractive sequence $w$ and for any $v\perp\mathbf{1}$ , it holds that

$$ \left\lVert M_{w}v\right\rVert\leqslant 2^{\kappa}\lambda^{\kappa-1}\lVert v\rVert\,. $$

#### Proof.

We will prove this claim by induction on $\kappa$ . For the base case of $\kappa=0$ , the statement follows from $\lVert v\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\lVert v\rVert$ .

For $\kappa\geqslant 1$ , let $v_{1}=\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}A_{1}D_{x}v$ and $v^{\prime}=\Pi_{\perp}A_{1}D_{x}v$ . These satisfy that $\lVert v_{1}\rVert\leqslant\lVert v\rVert$ and $\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert=\lVert\Pi_{\perp}A_{1}D_{x}v\rVert=\lVert A_{1}\Pi_{\perp}D_{x}v\rVert\leqslant\lambda\lVert v\rVert$ , where we use that $A_{1}$ and $\Pi_{\perp}$ commute since $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenspace of $A_{1}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=1}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)v\right\rVert \displaystyle\leqslant\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=2}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)v_{1}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=2}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)v^{\prime}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leqslant(2\lambda)^{\kappa-1}\lVert v_{1}\rVert+2^{\kappa-1}\lambda^{\kappa-2}\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert \displaystyle\leqslant(2\lambda)^{\kappa-1}\lVert v\rVert+2^{\kappa-1}\lambda^{\kappa-2}\cdot\lambda\lVert v\rVert \displaystyle=2^{\kappa}\lambda^{\kappa-1}\lVert v\rVert, $$

where we use in the second inequality Lemma 2.17 for the contractive subsequence $(w_{2},\dots,w_{\kappa})$ to bound $\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=2}^{\kappa}A_{j}D_{x}\right)v_{1}\right\rVert$ and the inductive hypothesis for $(w_{2},\dots,w_{\kappa})$ to bound $\left\lVert\left(\prod_{j=2}^{a}A_{j}D_{x}\right)v^{\prime}\right\rVert$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 2.16.

Let $v$ be any vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}}$ , and let $v_{1}=\Pi_{\mathbf{1}}v$ and $v^{\prime}=\Pi_{\perp}v$ . Combining the bounds from Lemmas 2.17 and 2.18, we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert M_{w}v\right\rVert \displaystyle\leqslant\left\lVert M_{w}v_{1}\right\rVert+\left\lVert M_{w}v^{\prime}\right\rVert\leqslant(2\lambda)^{\kappa}\lVert v_{1}\rVert+2^{\kappa}\lambda^{\kappa-1}\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert\leqslant 2^{\kappa+1}\lambda^{\kappa-1}\lVert v\rVert\,.\qed $$

## 3 Free Expanders

In our construction of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes, we use explicit constructions of “free expanders” given by O’Donnell and Wu [26] that satisfy the all-signings near-Ramanujan property (Definition 2.3). However, their construction is significantly more general. In this section, we describe their result, highlight some additional properties and show several applications of their result.

To describe their construction, we will need the notion of a noncommutative polynomial and a free group. Let $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ denote the set of all words of length $\leqslant k$ on self-adjoint indeterminates $Y_{1},\dots,Y_{D}$ , i.e. $Y_{i}=Y_{i}^{*}$ . A noncommutative polynomial of degree $\leqslant k$ on these indeterminates can generally be written as:

$$ P(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{D})=\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{k}}\widehat{P}_{W}W\,, $$

for $\widehat{P}_{W}\in\mathbb{R}$ . We say that a polynomial is self-adjoint is $P^{*}=P$ , and define the Frobenius norm of a polynomial as $\left\lVert P\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{k}}|\widehat{P}_{W}|^{2}}$ .

Let $F_{D}$ be the free group on $D$ self-adjoint generators $x_{1},\dots,x_{D}$ such that $x_{i}^{2}=1$ . We identify elements of the free group via their adjacency operators—formally, we identify $g\in F_{D}$ as a linear operator on $\ell_{2}(F_{D})\coloneqq\left\{f:F_{D}\to\mathbb{R}\mid\sum_{g\in F_{D}}f(g)^{2}<\infty\right\}$ where $gf(u)=f(gu)$ .

A key result of interest from [26] is on the existence of an infinite family of finite matching matrices that spectrally approximate the free group for all low-degree polynomials.

#### Theorem 3.1 ([26, Special case of Theorem 10.13]).

For every $D,k\geqslant 1$ , and $r,\varepsilon>0$ , there is an algorithm that takes in a positive integer input $N$ , and in $\mathrm{poly}(N)$ time outputs perfect matching matrices $X_{1},\dots,X_{D}$ of dimension $N^{\prime}\times N^{\prime}$ where $N^{\prime}=N+o(N)$ , such that simultaneously for every degree- $\leqslant k$ self-adjoint polynomial $P(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{D})$ such that $\left\lVert P\right\rVert_{F}\leqslant r$ , we have:

$$ \mathrm{Spec}\left\lparen p(X_{1},\dots,X_{D})\big|_{\mathbf{1}^{\perp}}\right\rparen\subseteq\mathrm{Spec}\left\lparen p(x_{1},\dots,x_{D})\right\rparen\pm[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\,. $$

The result of [26] also applies to polynomials with matrix-valued coefficients, which is relevant to constructing expanding lifts of fixed constant-sized expander graphs.

#### Remark 3.2 (Near-Ramanujan graphs).

Observe that choosing $P(X_{1},\dots,X_{D})=\sum_{i=1}^{D}X_{i}$ yields a $D$ -regular graph whose spectrum approximates that of $\sum_{i=1}^{D}x_{i}$ , which is the adjacency operator of the $D$ -regular infinite tree whose spectrum is $[-2\sqrt{D-1},2\sqrt{D-1}]$ . Therefore, the construction yields a near-Ramanujan graph.

#### Remark 3.3 (All-signings near-Ramanujan family).

We may obtain Theorem 2.4 as a corollary of Theorem 3.1 by choosing $D=dt$ , and restricting our attention to the collection of signed linear combinations of $X_{1},\dots,X_{D}$ . The graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ can be chosen by picking $H_{i}\coloneqq X_{d(i-1)+1}+\dots+X_{di}$ . The spectrum of any signed linear combination of $x_{1},\dots,x_{D}$ is $[-2\sqrt{D-1},2\sqrt{D-1}]$ .

### 3.1 Lossless Expanders on Average

We say that a $d$ -regular graph $G=(V,E)$ is a lossless expander if every subset $S\subseteq V$ of size at most $\eta|V|$ (where $\eta$ depends only on $d$ ) has at least $(1-\varepsilon)d|S|$ distinct neighbors, with arbitrarily small $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(d)\to 0$ as $d\to\infty$ . The explicit construction of constant-degree lossless expanders has been a long-standing open question [13], and this was recently resolved in a line of work [16, 14, 15].

Using [26], we can construct a collection of $d$ -regular graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ on the same vertex set that are “lossless expanders on average”, meaning that any small subset $S\subseteq V$ has lossless expansion in most graphs among $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ . The specific property we need is stated below, which follows from Theorem 3.1 and [9, §2.2, Eq. (10)].

#### Theorem 3.4.

For every integer $t\geqslant 1$ and $d\geqslant 2$ , there is an explicit construction of $d$ -regular graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ on the same vertex set such that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm 1\}^{t}}\left\lVert\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sigma_{j}\left\lparen A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}\right\rparen^{\perp}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant O\left\lparen\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}\cdot d}\right\rparen\,, $$

where $A_{j}=\frac{1}{d}\mathrm{Adj}(H_{j})$ is the normalized adjacency matrix of $H_{j}$ , and $A_{j}^{\perp}$ is the matrix with the $\bm{1}$ eigenspace removed.

Intuitively, $A_{j}^{2}$ is the transition matrix of $2$ -step walks on $H_{j}$ , which has a $\frac{1}{d}$ probability of going back to the starting vertex. Thus, $A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}$ is the transition matrix of $2$ -step non-backtracking walks on $H_{j}$ , and Theorem 3.4 can be viewed as the all-signings near-Ramanujan property of such walks.

With Theorem 3.4, we show the following.

#### Theorem 3.5 (Lossless expanders on average).

Let $d,t\in\mathbb{N}$ . There is an explicit construction of $d$ -regular graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ on vertex set $V$ that satisfy the following: let $\varepsilon,\eta,\gamma\in(0,1)$ such that $\eta\leqslant O(\gamma\varepsilon/d)$ and $t\geqslant\Omega(\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}\varepsilon^{2}})$ , then for any subset $S\subseteq V$ of size $|S|\leqslant\eta|V|$ , at least $1-\gamma$ fraction of $j\in[t]$ has $|N_{j}(S)|\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)d|S|$ .

#### Proof.

We will show that the graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ from Theorem 3.4 satisfy lossless expansion on average. Fix a subset $S\subseteq V$ of size at most $\eta n$ . Consider the quadratic form $\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}$ , where $\bm{1}_{S}$ is the 0-1 indicator vector of $S$ . Since $A_{j}$ is the normalized adjacency matrix of $H_{j}$ , $\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}$ equals $\frac{1}{d^{2}}$ times the number of length- $2$ walks that start and end in $S$ . Since a length- $2$ walk can be described by choosing the middle vertex $v$ , and picking two (possibly identical) neighbors of $v$ in $S$ , we may write the number of length- $2$ walks that start and end in $S$ as $\sum_{v\in N_{j}(S)}d_{j,v}^{2}$ , where $d_{j,v}=|E_{H_{j}}(v,S)|$ . Thus, we may write

$$ \displaystyle\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}=\frac{1}{d^{2}}\sum_{v\in N_{j}(S)}d_{j,v}^{2}=\frac{|N_{j}(S)|}{d^{2}}\cdot\mathbf{E}_{v\in N_{j}(S)}[d_{j,v}^{2}]\geqslant\frac{|N_{j}(S)|}{d^{2}}\cdot\mathbf{E}_{v\sim N_{j}(S)}[d_{j,v}]^{2}\,, $$

where $N_{j}(S)$ refers to the neighborhood of $S$ in $H_{j}$ . Observe that $\sum_{v\in N_{j}(S)}d_{j,v}$ is equal to the number of edges from $S$ to $N_{j}(S)$ , which is equal to $d|S|$ . Thus, $\mathbf{E}_{v\sim N_{j}(S)}[d_{j,v}]=\frac{d|S|}{|N_{j}(S)|}$ , and we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}\geqslant\frac{|N_{j}(S)|}{d^{2}}\cdot\frac{d^{2}|S|^{2}}{|N_{j}(S)|^{2}}=\frac{|S|^{2}}{|N_{j}(S)|}\,. $$

On the other hand, writing $\bm{1}_{S}=\frac{|S|}{n}\bm{1}+\bm{1}_{S}^{\perp}$ where $\bm{1}_{S}^{\perp}$ is orthogonal to $\bm{1}$ , we have $\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}=\frac{|S|^{2}}{n}+\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}(A_{j}^{2})^{\perp}\bm{1}_{S}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\left\lvert\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}\left\lparen A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}\right\rparen\bm{1}_{S}\right\rvert \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{|S|^{2}}{n}+\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm 1\}^{t}}\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sigma_{j}\cdot\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}\left\lparen A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\right\rparen^{\perp}\bm{1}_{S} \displaystyle\leqslant\eta|S|+|S|\cdot\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm 1\}^{t}}\left\lVert\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sigma_{j}\left\lparen A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}\right\rparen^{\perp}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leqslant|S|\cdot\left\lparen\eta+O\left\lparen\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}d}\right\rparen\right\rparen\,, $$

where the last inequality follows from the guarantee of Theorem 3.4. By Markov’s inequality, at least $1-\gamma$ fraction of $j\in[t]$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}\left\lparen A_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}\right\rparen\bm{1}_{S}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{|S|}{d}\cdot\left\lparen\frac{\eta d}{\gamma}+O\left\lparen\frac{1}{\gamma\sqrt{t}}\right\rparen\right\rparen\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon|S|}{d}\,, $$

as long as $\eta\leqslant O(\gamma\varepsilon/d)$ and $t\geqslant\Omega(\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}\varepsilon^{2}})$ . Combined with the lower bound $\bm{1}_{S}^{\top}A_{j}^{2}\bm{1}_{S}\geqslant\frac{|S|^{2}}{|N_{j}(S)|}$ , we have that $1-\gamma$ fraction of $j\in[t]$ satisfies

$$ \frac{|S|^{2}}{|N_{j}(S)|}\leqslant\frac{|S|}{d}(1+\varepsilon)\implies|N_{j}(S)|\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)d|S|\,.\qed $$

### 3.2 Explicit Rotating Expanders

One of the sources of suboptimality in our construction as well as previous work [27, 7] is the factor of $2$ per step on a Ramanujan graph. If one were to obtain an explicit construction of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes achieving the GV bound without an $\varepsilon^{o(1)}$ overhead in the rate based on expander walks, it would be necessary to circumvent the fact that the operator norm of the adjacency matrix of any Ramanujan graph has spectral radius $\approx\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ , as opposed to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}$ .

In the context of mixing of random walks, it has been observed that this factor of $2$ can be shaved if one performs a nonbacktracking walk on a Ramanujan graph [2]. Cohen and Maor [8] used the method of interlacing polynomials and finite free probability (cf. [22]) to exhibit the existence of “rotating expanders”: a sequence of $d$ -regular (one-sided) Ramanujan graphs $G_{1},\dots,G_{\ell}$ such that the second eigenvalue of $G_{1}\cdot G_{2}\cdots G_{\ell}\cdot G_{\ell}\cdot G_{\ell-1}\cdots G_{1}$ is at most $O(\ell)\cdot d^{-\ell}$ , as opposed to $2^{2\ell}d^{-\ell}$ . Moreover, they can guarantee that each $G_{i}$ is a relabeling of $G_{1}$ .

We observe below that an explicit sequence of expanders satisfying this property can be obtained from Theorem 3.1. In particular, by combining Theorem 3.1 and a result of Haagerup [12, Lemma 1.4], we have the following.

#### Theorem 3.6.

Fix $d,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ . There is an explicit construction of $d$ -regular graphs $H_{1},\dots,H_{t}$ on the same vertex set such that each $H_{j}$ satisfies $\|A_{H_{j}}^{\perp}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}}$ , and moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\left\lparen A_{H_{\ell}}A_{H_{\ell-1}}\cdots A_{H_{1}}\right\rparen^{\perp}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant O(\ell)\cdot d^{-\ell/2}\,. $$

Further, it is possible to realize $H_{i}$ as $P_{i}H_{1}P_{i}^{\top}$ for a permutation matrix $P_{i}$ .

Note that the naive bound in this case is $2^{\ell}d^{-\ell/2}$ , and this would be tight if all the graphs are identical. On the other hand, $A_{H_{\ell}}A_{H_{\ell-1}}\cdots A_{H_{1}}$ is the transition matrix of $\ell$ -step walks on $d$ -regular graphs, which can be viewed as the transition matrix of a $d^{\ell}$ -regular graph. If this graph were Ramanujan, we would get a bound of $2\cdot d^{-\ell/2}$ .

In the context of $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes, it remains unclear how the factor of $2^{\ell}$ can be removed in the setting of Equation 1, where one inserts a diagonal matrix $D_{x}$ between consecutive $A_{H_{i}}$ . However, we hope that this phenomenon will one day lead to improved analysis of such expander walks, yielding explicit $\varepsilon$ -balanced codes closer to the GV bound.
